### 1.1 One-carbon metabolism

Introduction to one-carbon metabolism

Folate lies at the core of one-carbon metabolism (1CM), serving as the essential carrier of one-

carbon (1C) units that fuel a wide range of biosynthetic and regulatory processes. In its various

reduced forms, folate accepts and donates methyl, methylene, methenyl, and formyl groups,

thereby enabling the metabolic reactions that constitute 1CM. Folate is indispensable for

nucleotide synthesis, providing the one-carbon units required for de novo purine formation and for

the thymidylate synthase reaction that generates dTMP. These are required to sustain replication

fork progression. Sufficient nucleotide availability supports efficient DNA synthesis and prevents

replication stress. Under conditions of insufficient folate, reduced dTMP and purine pools lead to

nucleotide imbalance, slowing replication fork progression and increasing the likelihood of fork

stalling or collapse. This can result in incomplete DNA replication, accumulation of DNA strand

breaks, and activation of DNA damage responses1.

Folate also supports amino acid metabolism by enabling the interconversion of serine and

glycine and sustaining methionine regeneration through the methionine cycle. In mitochondria,

folate-dependent 1C reactions supply formyl groups necessary for mitochondrial translation

initiation and contribute to redox balance and energy metabolism, underscoring its central role in

maintaining cellular and organellar function2, 3. Thus, folate availability directly shapes the

capacity of cells to maintain growth, genome stability, and oxidative homeostasis. By generating

key 1CM intermediates, folate availability shapes the fidelity and kinetics of protein synthesis,

including in the mitochondria where 1CM-derived metabolites modulate translation initiation 4.

Because these folate-driven reactions underpin nucleotide production and amino acid

interconversion, both 1CM and the 1C carrier folate are indispensable for all cells. Unlike


<!-- Page 11 -->


3

microbes, yeast, and plants, animals cannot synthesize folate de novo and instead rely entirely on

dietary folate. This dependency makes extracellular folate supply crucial for cellular viability in

both proliferating and non-dividing tissues, with rapidly dividing cells being especially sensitive

due to their heightened need for RNA and DNA synthesis2.

Folate as 1C carriers

Folate molecules act as carriers of 1C units, enabling their transfer and transformation for

essential metabolic reactions (Fig. 1.1). These 1C groups are covalently attached to

tetrahydrofolate (THF) at two sites: the N5 position of the pteridine ring and the N10 position of

the p-aminobenzoate moiety. Depending on how they are bound, 1C units can exist in three distinct

oxidation states, each serving specialized biosynthetic functions. Most 1C units enter the pathway

as 5,10-methylene-THF, generated primarily from the amino acids serine and glycine, as well as

from choline catabolites dimethylglycine and sarcosine. Because folates carrying 1C units cannot

freely cross intracellular membranes, 5,10-methylene-THF must be produced in both the

mitochondria and cytosol to support its role as a carbon donor in reactions that take place in both

compartments5. Once attached to THF, these 1C groups can be interconverted between oxidation

states, with 5,10-methylene-THF, 5-methyl-THF, and 10-formyl-THF supporting distinct

metabolic reactions. An additional folate species, 5-formyl-THF, does not directly participate in

biosynthesis but serves as a storage reserve of 1C units2, 6.

Folate and nucleotide synthesis

Within the folate cycle, distinct folate cofactors support nucleotide formation: 10-formyl-

THF donates formyl groups for de novo purine synthesis, while 5,10-methylene-THF fuels the

thymidylate synthase reaction in the pyrimidine pathway. Purine synthesis pathways are relevant

for the projects described in this thesis because disruptions in one-carbon metabolism, via folate

depletion or pharmacologic inhibition, impairs purine synthesis quickly due to the high flux in the

pathway and the requirement for 2-10 formyl THF molecules, making purine synthesis a reliable

readout of folate deprivation. Since purines are essential building blocks of DNA and RNA, as

well as key components of the energy carriers ATP and GTP, any limitation in their synthesis can

have widespread effects on cellular proliferation, gene expression, and energy metabolism.

De novo purine synthesis constructs purine nucleotides from basic precursors. The 11-

reaction process begins with the formation of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP), followed by

the addition of glutamine to generate 5-phosphoribosylamine, and proceeds through multiple

reactions to produce inosine monophosphate (IMP). IMP then serves as a key intermediate that is

subsequently converted into the final purine nucleotides, adenosine monophosphate (AMP) and

guanosine monophosphate (GMP)2.

Importantly, de novo purine nucleotide synthesis includes two folate-dependent

transformylase reactions. These are catalyzed by 5′-phosphoribosyl-glycinamide (GAR)

transformylase and 5′-phosphoribosyl-5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide (AICAR)

transformylase, which insert carbon 8 and carbon 2, respectively, into the purine ring. Both

enzymes require 10-formyltetrahydrofolate as the donor of the 1C unit8(Fig. 1.2).

Separately, via the pyrimidine pathway, thymidylate synthase catalyzes the conversion of

dUMP to dTMP, the only de novo route for cellular thymidylate production (Fig. 1.2b). This

reaction depends on 5,10-methylene-THF, which donates the one-carbon unit that becomes the

methyl group incorporated into dTMP. During this transfer, 5,10-methylene-THF is oxidized to

dihydrofolate (DHF), directly coupling thymidylate synthesis to folate metabolism. Because DNA

replication and repair require a continuous supply of dTMP, loss of thymidylate synthase activity

arrests cellular proliferation and triggers cell death9, 10.

The interconnection of the folate cycle, methionine cycle, and the transsulfuration pathway

1CM is comprised of the folate cycle, methionine cycle, and the transsulfuration pathway.

The methionine cycle serves as the central framework of methionine metabolism, comprising a

series of reactions responsible for both the breakdown and regeneration of methionine. It operates

in close association with the folate cycle, together forming the two major arms of 1CM (Fig. 1.2c).

A key output of the methionine cycle is the production of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM),

the universal methyl donor that fuels cellular methylation reactions. The methylation cycle is

organized around the continuous production, utilization, and regeneration of SAM, the universal

methyl donor. Extracellular methionine, imported primarily through solute carrier (SLC)

transporters, enters the cycle when methionine adenosyltransferases (MATs) convert it into SAM

using ATP. MAT1A operates predominantly in the liver, whereas MAT2A and MAT2B are

broadly expressed in non-hepatic tissues. The SAM produced by these enzymes fuels a wide range

of methyltransferases that methylate DNA, RNA, histones, proteins, and lipids. After SAM

donates its methyl group, it is converted to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH). SAH is then

hydrolyzed by adenosylhomocysteinase (AHCY) to form homocysteine; however, this reaction is


<!-- Page 17 -->


9

reversible, and increased homocysteine can drive the equilibrium backward, leading to SAH

accumulation. Because SAH is a potent inhibitor of SAM-dependent methyltransferases, its

buildup lowers the cell’s effective methylation capacity. The balance between SAM and SAH

(reflected as a SAM/SAH ratio) therefore serves as a key indicator of cellular methylation

potential. Completion of the cycle requires remethylation of homocysteine to regenerate

methionine. In liver and kidney, betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT) catalyzes this

reaction using betaine as the methyl donor, whereas most other tissues rely on folate-dependent

methionine synthase. Together, these steps maintain methionine recycling and sustain intracellular

SAM pools11.

The transsulfuration pathway is a key component of cellular sulfur metabolism and redox

homeostasis. In mammals, it facilitates the transfer of sulfur from homocysteine to cysteine

through the intermediate cystathionine and represents the sole endogenous route for cysteine

biosynthesis. Homocysteine, produced from dietary methionine, is first converted by cystathionine

β-synthase (CBS) into cystathionine, and subsequently cleaved by cystathionine γ-lyase (CSE) to

yield cysteine12, 13. Beyond its fundamental role in protein synthesis, cysteine serves as a precursor

for glutathione (GSH), which is the cell’s primary antioxidant, and acts as a potent antioxidant

itself. Disruptions in cysteine or GSH metabolism are strongly associated with oxidative stress,

redox imbalance, and neurodegenerative disorders14, 15. Both CBS and CSE are central regulators

of this redox network, and studies estimate that roughly half of the cysteine generated through this

pathway in hepatic tissue is utilized for GSH synthesis16, 17. Cysteine also serves as the substrate

for the production of hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) and other sulfur-containing metabolites18. In addition,

it is converted into taurine via the enzyme cysteine dioxygenase (CDO), which oxidizes cysteine

to cysteinesulfinic acid. This intermediate is then decarboxylated by cysteinesulfinic acid


<!-- Page 18 -->


10

decarboxylase to form hypotaurine, which is further oxidized to taurine19. Because CDO directly

acts on cysteine, it influences H₂S production by regulating cysteine availability. Taurine itself

contributes to a wide range of physiological processes, including osmoregulation, immune and

neural modulation, calcium signaling, visual function, and antioxidant defense20. Finally, the

transsulfuration and transmethylation pathways are closely interconnected via homocysteine,

which can either be remethylated to regenerate methionine or irreversibly converted into

cysteine21.

### 1.2 One-carbon metabolism perturbation in disease

Folate in public health

Folate deficiency is a nutritional disorder that carries important clinical and public health

consequences, it is most prevalent in underdeveloped countries. It can arise from inadequate

dietary intake, impaired absorption, increased physiological demand, or interference from certain

medications, and is defined by reduced folate levels in serum, plasma, or red blood cells. Left

uncorrected, folate deficiency contributes to megaloblastic anemia, neuropsychiatric

manifestations, and serious pregnancy complications, most notably neural tube defects in the

developing fetus.

Adequate folic acid intake during the periconceptional period is a well-established

preventive measure to lower the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs). NTDs arise from failure of

the neural tube to close properly during early embryonic development, leaving the underlying

neural tissue exposed and vulnerable to damage. These defects are associated with substantial

morbidity and mortality, depending on the site and severity of the lesion. Anencephaly is the most


<!-- Page 19 -->


11

severe form and incompatible with life, whereas lower spinal lesions characteristic of spina bifida

can lead to serious complications such as urinary and fecal incontinence and paralysis of the lower

limbs22. Early randomized controlled trials demonstrated that folic acid (FA) supplementation

prevents both recurrent and first-occurrence NTDs, leading the U.S. Public Health Service in 1992

to recommend that all women of childbearing age consume at least 400 µg daily. However,

adherence to supplementation can be limited by physician counseling, low supplement use, and

the high proportion of unplanned pregnancies. To address this, the U.S. Food and Drug

Administration (FDA) mandated in 1998 that enriched cereal-grain products (i.e., wheat flour,

maize flour, or rice) be fortified with 140 µg FA per 100 g of flour. Although several medical and

advocacy groups argued for a higher fortification level (350 µg/100 g) to maximize NTD

prevention, they supported the lower level to avoid delays in implementation, anticipating future

reassessment. Since then, fortification has been widely recognized as a major public health

achievement, however not without debate regarding whether higher fortification could yield

additional reductions in NTDs without causing harm23. For example, more recent studies

performed in mice indicate that an excess of folate may be detrimental to fetal development, such

as in altering neurogenesis in the brain24, 25. In mouse models, excessive folic acid intake led to

long-term structural changes in cortical neurons, notably reduced dendritic branching of deep-layer

projection neurons26. These findings highlight the importance of balanced micronutrient status in

supporting a healthy neurodevelopment.

Populations at greatest risk include individuals with lower education, young women, and

those with unplanned pregnancies. In countries without mandatory fortification, most people fail

to meet the recommended daily intake of 0.4 mg of folate from food sources. By contrast,

mandatory flour fortification in the United States has markedly improved folate status and reduced


<!-- Page 20 -->


12

NTD rates by a reported ~20-50% in the decade after implementation27, 28. More recent numbers

for spina bifida, anencephaly, and encephalocele in the U.S. are 1,300, 700, and 350 babies per

year, respectively29. Despite this success, many countries (particularly in the eastern hemisphere,

primarily countries in Asia and Africa) have not adopted mandatory fortification, citing the lack

of definitive evidence for broader health benefits, concerns about potential risks, and issues of

personal choice (Figure 1.3). As a result, the global burden of NTDs remains an ongoing challenge

that requires continued attention, including through targeted public health initiatives to improve

folate status29.

In addition to NTDs, folate deficiency in pregnancy is additionally associated with a

significantly increased risk of preterm delivery, stunted fetal growth, miscarriage, placental

abruption, and severe language delays in the child30.

Pathological consequences of 1CM perturbation via folate depletion

Drugs that inhibit 1CM in bacteria, such as sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, or in

mammals, such as methotrexate and pemetrexed, are extensively used as antibiotics, and

anticancer agents. In addition, folate-targeting therapies are administered to millions of individuals

with rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune disorders to limit inappropriate immune cell

proliferation and activation, reflecting folate’s essential role in hematopoiesis and cell growth.

Despite the widespread use of agents that interfere with 1CM, the molecular processes underlying

how cells adapt to disruptions are still being investigated.

Extensive research carried out, especially during the 1960s through 1980s, was

instrumental in defining the 1CM enzymes through a combination of biochemical, kinetic, and

structural approaches. During this period, investigators purified enzymes such as dihydrofolate

reductase (DHFR), serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT), and methylenetetrahydrofolate

dehydrogenase/cyclohydrolase from mammalian and microbial sources, enabling detailed analysis

of their catalytic properties and cofactor requirements32, 33. The use of 13C-labeled one-carbon

units allowed researchers to map the flow of one-carbon units through folate derivatives, directly

linking specific enzymatic steps to nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis34, 35. In parallel,

advances in enzyme kinetics and inhibition studies clarified regulatory features of the pathway,

including feedback mechanisms and sensitivity to antifolate drugs such as methotrexate, which

further confirmed the central role of DHFR in maintaining tetrahydrofolate pools36, 37. Subcellular

fractionation experiments revealed that components of the 1CM pathway operate in both cytosolic

and mitochondrial compartments, highlighting the compartmentalized nature of folate

metabolism38.

### 1.3 Cellular pathology following one-carbon metabolism perturbation


<!-- Page 23 -->


15

1CM is essential for cellular proliferation

Because 1CM provides essential intermediates for nucleotide production, its inhibition has

a direct impact on cell proliferation. Folate-mediated reactions within this pathway generate key

1C donors, including 10-formyl-THF for purine biosynthesis and 5,10-methylene-THF for

thymidylate (dTMP) formation. 1CM disruption through nutrient deficiency or antifolate treatment

reduces the availability of these intermediates, leading to imbalances in nucleotide pools and

impaired DNA synthesis. A critical consequence is the insufficient production of dTMP, which

promotes the incorporation of uracil into DNA and induces DNA damage during repair processes.

At the same time, decreased purine synthesis limits the generation of ATP and GTP, further

restricting nucleic acid synthesis and cellular energy supply. These metabolic deficiencies trigger

replication fork collapse and activate cell cycle checkpoints, particularly during S-phase, often

resulting in growth arrest or programmed cell death. Furthermore, since the mitochondrial 1CM

produces NADH and NADPH, inhibition of 1CM leads to increased oxidative stress, triggering

DNA damage and the DNA damage response (DDR). In this way, inhibition of 1CM suppresses

proliferation by undermining both the biochemical building blocks (nucleotide synthesis

deficiencies) and metabolic requirements for DNA replication1.

1CM is essential for gene expression

Folate is also essential for the regulation of gene expression through epigenetic

mechanisms such as DNA methylation, gene silencing, and histone modification. It functions as a

key one-carbon donor in the methylation cycle, converting homocysteine into methionine, which

is then converted into SAM. SAM provides the necessary methyl groups for DNA

methyltransferases (DNMTs). DNMTs can methylate CpG islands in promoter regions, causing 5-


<!-- Page 24 -->


16

methylcytosine formation and resulting in epigenetic silencing of gene expression39. Histone

methylation is also supported by 1CM through SAM, affecting the accessibility of genes for

transcription39, 40.

1.4 One-carbon metabolism and translation 1CM is interconnected with translation

1CM regulates translation in part through the production of SAM, which serves as a methyl

donor for the methylation of rRNA, tRNA, mRNA, and translation factors, thereby influencing

multiple steps of protein synthesis. In addition, 1CM is closely interconnected with amino acid

and redox networks, further linking its activity to ribosome function and the translational

efficiency. The pathway is functionally coupled to serine and glycine metabolism, which not only

supply 1C units but also contribute to the intracellular amino acid pool required for translation.

Changes in serine availability can influence nutrient-sensing pathways, including mTOR

signaling, thereby affecting ribosome biogenesis and overall translational output. Furthermore,

folate-dependent reactions within 1CM contribute to NADPH production, supporting cellular

redox homeostasis. This is important for maintaining ribosomal function and enabling sustained

protein synthesis, particularly under conditions of metabolic stress. Together, these interactions

highlight the role of 1CM in coordinating the metabolic environment necessary for efficient

translation2, 41.

1CM and nutrient sensing in regulating translation


<!-- Page 25 -->


17

1CM is closely linked to nutrient-sensing pathways that regulate translation, in part through

its dependence on amino acid availability and its role in generating S-adenosylmethionine, which

influences methylation and growth signaling pathways such as mTOR2, 41.

Cells rely on environmentally available nutrients to sustain metabolism and support

essential biological functions. Because nutrient availability can fluctuate considerably, cells must

continually adjust their gene expression in response to these changes. One key mechanism

underlying this adaptability is the regulation of translation, with the mTOR pathway serving as a

central controller42.

Purine availability regulates mTORC1 signaling indirectly through the TSC-RHEB axis, a

central pathway that integrates cellular metabolic status and stress signals. Under conditions where

purine nucleotide levels are sufficient, RHEB remains in its active, GTP-bound form and supports

mTORC1 activation at the lysosomal surface43. In contrast, when purine synthesis is compromised,

as occurs when when 1CM is inhibited, declining nucleotide pools cause metabolic stress that

activates the TSC complex (TSC1/2). As a GTPase-activating protein, the TSC complex

inactivates RHEB by promoting its GDP-bound state, thereby suppressing mTORC1 activity.

Furthermore, reduced purine availability can diminish cellular energy via ATP/GTP, contributing

to activation of AMPK, which acts upstream of mTORC1 and reinforces its inhibition in part

through TSC244. Collectively, these mechanisms illustrate that mTORC1 responds to the

metabolic consequences of purine depletion.

Through its downstream effectors, mTORC1 plays a major role in regulating translation.

mTORC1 functions as a central regulator of protein synthesis by coordinating translation initiation

with growth factor signaling, nutrient availability, and cellular energy status41. It promotes

translational activity in part by phosphorylating key downstream effectors, including eIF4E-


<!-- Page 26 -->


18

binding proteins (4E-BPs) and ribosomal S6 kinases (S6K1/2). Phosphorylation of 4E-BPs causes

their release from eIF4E, enabling formation of the eIF4F complex, a critical and rate-limiting step

in cap-dependent translation initiation. Concurrently, activation of S6K enhances translation

through phosphorylation of targets such as ribosomal protein S6 and eIF4B, which support

ribosome function and mRNA recruitment. mTORC1 also selectively promotes the translation of

mRNAs containing 5′ terminal oligopyrimidine (TOP) motifs, many of which encode components

of the translational machinery, including ribosomal proteins and elongation factors45. Through

these mechanisms, mTORC1 links environmental inputs to the control of protein synthesis, with

its activity being suppressed under conditions of nutrient limitation or cellular stress. In this way,

mTORC1 links nutrient and metabolic status (including purine availability) to the dialing of

translational capacity.

However, recent studies indicate that translation is not solely governed by external

regulators of the ribosome, such as mTOR signaling and initiation factors, but also by alterations

in ribosomal composition itself46, 47.

Some unanswered questions in folate biology

Since folate was first identified, major advances have been made in the characterization of

folate and 1CM. Recent studies have revealed new regulatory mechanisms and condition-specific

differences in 1CM, but important knowledge gaps remain. 1CM enzymes are not expressed

uniformly across tissues and cell types, the effects of nutrient availability are still being explored,

and how nutrient states and cellular signals are integrated through transcription and post-

translationally.


<!-- Page 27 -->


19

In addition, the role of 1CM in regulating cell proliferation, as well as its distinct

contributions to cell survival, remains an active area of investigation, particularly in the context of

changing nutrient levels. As how cells sense these nutrient changes and connect them to signaling

pathways, including transcriptional, translational, and post-translational regulation, is not yet fully

understood.

Although there is increasing evidence that 1CM influences processes beyond nucleotide

synthesis, such as epigenetic regulation and protein translation, the mechanisms behind these roles

remain incompletely defined. Overall, these gaps highlight the need for a more complete

understanding of how folate metabolism is regulated in different biological contexts and how it

supports cellular function in both health and disease.

### 2.1 Introduction

2.1.1 Megaloblastic anemia

Nutritional anemia represents a significant global health burden, with an estimated

prevalence of 24.3% in 2021, corresponding to approximately 1.92 billion individuals worldwide1.

Globally, folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies remain the most common causes, though in many

developed countries the prevalence of folate deficiency has decreased due to folic acid fortification

of foods2, 3.

Megaloblastic anemia represents a specific form of nutritional anemia, a broader group of

disorders caused by deficiencies in key nutrients required for red blood cell production. Although

nutritional anemias most frequently include iron deficiency, each condition disrupts erythropoiesis

through different biological mechanisms. Megaloblastic anemia arises specifically from

insufficient folate and/or vitamin B12, both of which are essential for one-carbon metabolism and

the synthesis of purines and thymidylate. A lack of these cofactors impairs DNA replication in

rapidly dividing precursor cells in the bone marrow, leading to abnormal nuclear maturation and

the formation of enlarged, immature erythroid cells known as megaloblasts. This defect is reflected

in the presence of macrocytic malfunctional red blood cells in circulation.

In comparison to iron deficiency anemia, which primarily compromises hemoglobin

production, megaloblastic anemia is characterized by defective DNA synthesis and disrupted cell

division. Thus, megaloblastic anemia is distinguished from other nutritional anemias by its

underlying metabolic basis and its characteristic cellular morphology4-6.

It has long been recognized that folate deficiency disrupts DNA synthesis, leading to

impaired replication. Folate deficiency limits the production of 5,10-methylene-THF, which is

required for thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis. As dTMP levels fall, uracil is misincorporated into


<!-- Page 35 -->


27

DNA, triggering repair cycles that cause strand breaks and stall replication forks. This slows DNA

synthesis, prolongs S-phase, and disrupts lagging-strand processes such as Okazaki fragment

joining. In hematopoietic precursors, these defects lead to failed cell division and cell cycle arrest

which are characteristic features of megaloblastic anemia7-9.

Key metabolic players

2.1.2 Regulation of nucleotide synthesis

Erythroid and erythroid progenitor cells turn over rapidly, resulting in an increased need

for nucleotide synthesis for DNA and RNA. Folate acts as a 1C donor and acceptor and is essential

for both purine and pyrimidine synthesis. In purine biosynthesis, 10-formyl tetrahydrofolate (THF)

contributes formyl groups at two steps of the pathway. In pyrimidine synthesis, 5,10-methylene

THF provides the 1C unit needed to convert deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) into

deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP)10.

As folate homeostasis and 1CM are essential for supporting normal cell function and

proliferation, these pathways are tightly regulated at the transcriptional and post-translational

levels, allowing cells to adapt to their environment. In particular, nutrient availability influences

cellular activity through a network of interconnected signaling cascades, including the mTOR,

PI3K, RAS, and AMPK pathways11-14.

The PI3K-AKT and RAS signaling pathways are central regulators of cellular responses to

nutrient availability and growth signals. Activation of PI3K-AKT promotes nutrient uptake and

anabolic metabolism, in part through activation of mTORC1. Similarly, RAS signaling supports

cell growth and proliferation by enhancing metabolic activity and protein synthesis. As a key

downstream integrator of these pathways, mTORC1 coordinates nutrient and energy status with


<!-- Page 36 -->


28

cellular processes such as translation, ribosome biogenesis, and cell growth. These signaling

networks function to allow cells to adjust their metabolic and biosynthetic activity in response to

environmental conditions.

AMPK functions as a central energy sensor that links cellular metabolic status to the

control of nucleotide biosynthesis. It detects an increased AMP/ATP or ADP/ATP ratio, which

reflects low energy availability, as well as upstream signaling from kinases such as LKB1 and

CaMKKβ in response to metabolic stress, hypoxia, or changes in intracellular calcium. These

signals activate AMPK when cellular energy is insufficient to support anabolic processes. AMPK

then responds by shifting cellular metabolism toward ATP-generating catabolic processes while

inhibiting ATP-consuming anabolic pathways15.

Activated AMPK suppresses nucleotide synthesis directly and indirectly through the

inhibition of anabolic pathways16. One key mechanism is the inhibition of mTORC1, which

reduces the expression and activity of enzymes involved in de novo purine and pyrimidine

synthesis. AMPK further limits biosynthesis by restricting metabolic flux into nucleotide

production by limiting precursor availability and reducing NADPH generation15. Through these

mechanisms, AMPK ensures that nucleotide synthesis, and therefore DNA replication and cell

proliferation, are reduced under conditions of energy stress.

2.1.3 A metabolic consequence of impaired 1CM

The link between AMPK signaling and 1CM is notable due to the role of AICAR, a purine

synthesis intermediate. During folate deficiency or 1CM perturbation, AICAR accumulates and

activates AMPK. Consequently, disruption of de novo purine synthesis leads to AICAR

accumulation, which in turn activates AMPK and suppresses further purine synthesis17.


<!-- Page 37 -->


29

2.1.4 Thymidylate synthesis

The pyrimidine biosynthesis pathway generates uridine monophosphate (UMP) and

proceeds largely independently of 1CM. UMP can be further converted into UTP, CTP, and dCTP

without requiring 1C units, supporting RNA and DNA synthesis. In contrast, the synthesis of

thymidylate (dTTP), which is specifically required for DNA replication, depends on 1CM.

Thymidylate synthase (TYMS) catalyzes the conversion of dUMP to dTMP using 5,10-methylene-

THF as a 1C donor, producing dihydrofolate (DHF) in the process. dTMP is subsequently

phosphorylated to dTDP and then dTTP through kinase reactions that do not require one-carbon

units. The DHF generated in this reaction is recycled back to tetrahydrofolate (THF) by

dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), allowing it to re-enter the folate pool. Thymidylate synthesis can

occur within a coordinated three-enzyme cycle involving SHMT, TYMS, and DHFR. These

enzymes have been proposed to form a nuclear complex during DNA replication and repair,

helping to maintain adequate thymidylate levels in the nucleus18. When dTTP levels are

insufficient, uracil is increasingly incorporated into DNA, leading to DNA damage through

repeated repair cycles19. This accumulation of DNA damage has been proposed as a key

mechanism underlying the molecular pathology of folate deficiency-induced anemia, linking folate

metabolism directly to effective hematopoiesis20.

2.1.5 Heme synthesis

Heme is an essential iron-containing molecule that plays a central role in numerous

biological processes. It functions as the prosthetic group in hemoglobin and myoglobin, enabling

oxygen transport and storage, and is also a critical component of cytochromes, catalases, heme

peroxidases, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Several forms of heme exist, with heme b being


<!-- Page 38 -->


30

the most abundant and the primary form incorporated into hemoglobin. Heme b also serves as the

precursor of other heme groups. Heme a, present in cytochrome a, and heme c, found in

cytochrome c, are both essential for oxidative phosphorylation within the mitochondrial electron

transport chain. Heme can be acquired through endogenous synthesis or via exogenous sources,

including intestinal absorption and intercellular transport.

Heme biosynthesis occurs through a tightly regulated process that takes place in both the

cytosol and the mitochondria. The pathway consists of eight enzymatic steps, which are initiated

and limited by 5′-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS), the rate-limiting enzyme of the pathway.

Two isoforms of ALAS exist: ALAS1, which is expressed ubiquitously in all cells, and ALAS2,

which is expressed primarily in erythroid precursor cells of the bone marrow as well as in

hepatocytes. The ALAS2 gene is located on the X chromosome, and its activity is specifically

adapted to the high demand for heme in red blood cell production.

The biosynthetic pathway begins in the mitochondria, where succinyl-CoA from the citric

acid cycle condenses with glycine to form δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) (Figure 2.1). This reaction

is catalyzed by ALAS in a pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)-dependent manner and represents the

rate-limiting step. ALA is then transported into the cytosol, where two molecules combine to form

porphobilinogen (PBG) via ALA dehydratase, a zinc-dependent enzyme. Four molecules of PBG

are subsequently polymerized into the linear tetrapyrrole hydroxymethylbilane (HMB) by

porphobilinogen deaminase, also known as hydroxymethylbilane synthase. HMB is then cyclized

by uroporphyrinogen III synthase to form uroporphyrinogen III, a critical step in the pathway, as

aberrant ring closure can lead to protoporphyria. Uroporphyrinogen III undergoes side-chain

modifications catalyzed by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, producing coproporphyrinogen III.

Coproporphyrinogen III is imported back into the mitochondria, where it is converted to


<!-- Page 39 -->


31

protoporphyrinogen IX by coproporphyrinogen oxidase. Protoporphyrinogen IX is then oxidized

by protoporphyrinogen oxidase to yield protoporphyrin IX. In the final step, ferrochelatase

catalyzes the insertion of ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) into protoporphyrin IX, generating heme. This final

product, ferrous protoporphyrin IX, forms the structural and functional basis of hemoproteins.

The chemical structure of heme b consists of a porphyrin ring composed of four pyrrole

units linked by methenyl bridges. Its side chains are arranged asymmetrically: methyl, vinyl,

methyl, and propionyl on rings A through C, and propionyl and methyl on ring D. This specific

arrangement underlies its distinct chemical reactivity and its critical role in oxygen binding and

electron transfer21.

2.1.6 Unanswered questions in folate-deficiency-induced anemia

In the 1940s researchers discovered that folate supplementation could correct

megaloblastic anemia. When patients with pernicious anemia were treated with folic acid, their

reticulocyte counts rose, accompanied by increases in hemoglobin levels and red blood cell

numbers22.

However, while impaired DNA synthesis and the loss of hematopoietic cells have been

implicated, the exact mechanism by which folate deficiency reduces hematopoiesis remains

unclear. Koury and Horne found in the 90s that proerythroblasts from folate-deficient mice

accumulated less folate and underwent apoptosis after partial differentiation and hemoglobin

synthesis, an effect that could be ameliorated using folic acid or thymidine but not by other

nucleosides. Their findings suggest that impaired thymidylate synthesis and consequent DNA

damage drive apoptosis, resulting in decreased red cell output, anemia, and a compensatory shift

toward earlier-stage erythroblasts in the bone marrow8, 23.

Despite these observations, the characteristic morphology of red blood cells in

megaloblastic anemia- enlarged and hemoglobin-rich- remains unexplained.  While impaired DNA

synthesis is central to current models, evidence that DNA chain elongation rates are largely

maintained under conditions of vitamin B12 deficiency or antifolate treatment in erythroid

progenitors suggests that this framework may not fully capture the underlying cellular

mechanisms24.

Folate-deprivation induced anemia has classically been ascribed to nucleotide depletion,

DNA damage, and increased apoptosis8, 23-26. However, studies evaluating DNA synthesis rates

have yielded inconsistent results, and these mechanisms alone do not adequately explain the

emergence of enlarged erythroid precursors or their elevated hemoglobin content. Thus, the


<!-- Page 42 -->


34

molecular basis of anemia caused by folate deficiency is still incompletely understood.

## Abstract

Folate, an essential vitamin, is a one‐carbon acceptor and donor in key metabolic reactions.

Erythroid cells harbor a unique sensitivity to folate deprivation, as revealed by the primary

pathological manifestation of nutritional folate deprivation: megaloblastic anemia. To study this

metabolic sensitivity, we applied mild folate depletion to human and mouse erythroid cell lines

and primary murine erythroid progenitors. We show that folate depletion induces early blockade

of purine synthesis and accumulation of the purine synthesis intermediate and signaling molecule,

5′‐phosphoribosyl‐5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide (AICAR), followed by enhanced heme

metabolism, hemoglobin synthesis, and erythroid differentiation. This is phenocopied by

inhibition of folate metabolism using the inhibitor SHIN1, and by AICAR supplementation.

Mechanistically, the metabolically driven differentiation is independent of mechanistic target of

rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and adenosine 5′‐monophosphateactivated protein kinase

(AMPK) and is instead mediated by protein kinase C. Our findings suggest that folate deprivation–

induced premature differentiation of erythroid progenitor cells is a molecular etiology to folate

deficiency–induced anemia.

## Introduction

Folic acid (FA) is a vitamin required for many cellular processes, including nucleotide

synthesis27, methylation28, and redox balance29, collectively known as one‐carbon (1C)

metabolism30. 1C metabolism requires the folate‐mediated transfer of methyl or formyl groups

from 1C donors, such as serine, to 1C acceptors, such as purine nucleotide intermediates31. Folate’s

role as the 1C unit carrier is essential in all cells; however, folate is not synthesized by mammalian

cells and must be consumed through the diet. Folate deficiency affects all cell types, but in

postembryonic tissues, it is especially detrimental to erythroid cells. This sensitivity is


<!-- Page 44 -->


36

demonstrated by the primary manifestation of nutritional folate deprivation anemia22.

Erythroid differentiation, or erythropoiesis, is the process that generates red blood cells

from multipotent hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow. During this multistep process,

progenitor cells go through several proliferation cycles to achieve abundant cell counts, while they

also decrease in size, increase hemoglobin synthesis, and undergo nuclear ejection on their way to

form mature erythrocytes. The differentiation program is tightly regulated and includes

multifaceted cellular changes that are orchestrated mainly by the transcription factors GATA‐

binding factor 1 (GATA1), Kruppel‐like factor 1 (KLF1), and Friend of GATA‐1 (FOG1)32. A

notable metabolic change during erythropoiesis is the up‐regulation of heme synthesis. Heme

synthesis starts with condensation of mitochondrial glycine with succinyl–coenzyme A (succinyl‐

CoA) by the rate limiting enzyme, 5‐aminolevulinic acid synthase 2 (ALAS2), to generate heme

in an eight‐step reaction. Glycine, which is a heme precursor, can be generated from serine in a

folate‐dependent reaction or through transport of extracellular glycine33.

The connection between folate and erythroid differentiation was revealed in the 1940s

when megaloblastic anemia was successfully treated with folate supplementation22. Early studies

that sought to understand the progression of folate‐deficient anemia suggested DNA damage‐

induced apoptosis as the mechanism for reduced erythrocytic cell counts8, 23. However, this

suggested mechanism does not fully support the appearance of large, hemoglobin‐rich, red blood

cells that are characteristic of megaloblastic anemia. This leaves the molecular etiology of

nutritional megaloblastic anemia unresolved.

We investigated the molecular etiology of nutritional anemia by studying the cellular

consequences of mild folate depletion in two erythrocytic cell lines: the human cell line K562 and

the murine erythroleukemia (MEL) cell line. We applied metabolite profiling and biochemical


<!-- Page 45 -->


37

assays to assess the metabolic changes and signaling events that occur following folate deprivation

in both cell lines. We found that in both cell lines, mild folate deprivation induced cell

differentiation in a mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and adenosine 5′‐

monophosphate–activated protein kinase (AMPK)–independent manner. We also excluded

blunted RAS signaling that we detected in these cells by RNA sequencing (RNA‐seq) as a key

signaling for the induction of low folate‐induced differentiation. However, we found that folate

deprivation–induced perturbation of purine metabolism is necessary for the induction of

differentiation. More specifically, the purine synthesis intermediate and signaling molecule 5′‐

phospho ribosyl‐5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide (AICAR), which accumulates rapidly upon

folate depletion, are necessary and sufficient for the differentiation phenotype. Moreover, we

found that protein kinase C (PKC), a kinase previously demonstrated to be activated by AICAR

34, is necessary for the observed differentiation in cell lines and primary murine erythroid

progenitor cells. We postulate a signaling axis that involves AICAR‐dependent activation of PKC,

which is a reported inducer of erythroid differentiation35-37. Our results suggest a molecular

etiology to folate deprivation–induced anemia: Early, aberrant progenitor differentiation can result

in low red blood cell counts due to reduced number of proliferation cycles and can also explain

the appearance of large, heme‐filled erythrocytes, both characteristic of megaloblastic anemia that

is caused by folate deprivation.

## Results

Folate depletion up-regulates heme synthesis and induces erythroid differentiation

Standard mammalian cell culture medium contains supraphysiological levels of most nutrients38.

RPMI and Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle medium (DMEM), two commonly used cell culture


<!-- Page 46 -->


38

medium, contain 2000 and 9000 nM FA (Gibco), respectively, while healthy adults have a plasma

folate concentration around 20 to 80 nM39, 40. Cell lines in culture are well adapted to this high

concentration of folate, and it is not detrimental to normal cell function. We sought to investigate

the metabolic changes in erythroid cells following a mild folate depletion, rather than complete

folate withdrawal, because this mild folate insufficiency is likely more similar to the stress induced

by nutritional folate deprivation that does not result in full systemic depletion of folate. We used

100 nM FA and compared this to the medium standard 2000 nM FA. This concentration led to a

modest proliferation defect of K562, a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line with the potential

to undergo erythroid differentiation (Fig. 2.3.2A)41, 42. Through metabolite profiling of 6‐day folate

deprived K562, we observed significant accumulation of the purine synthesis intermediates 5′‐

phosphoribosyl‐glycinamide (GAR) and AICAR (Fig. 2.3.2, B and C). These two metabolites are

substrates for reactions that require 10‐formyl tetrahydrofolate (THF) (Fig. 2.3.2B) and are

expected to become the rate limiting steps of de novo purine synthesis upon folate depletion43.

Several nucleotide salvage intermediates, including hypoxanthine, inosine, and guanosine, were

depleted under low FA conditions (Fig. 2.3.2C), as these can be used to regenerate inosine

monophosphate (IMP) levels when purine synthesis is impaired44. Unexpectedly, we also observed

a significant increase in intracellular heme, as well as accumulation of the last intermediate of

heme synthesis, protoporphyrin IX (Fig. 2.3.2, C and D). To test whether heme synthesis is actively

enhanced in folate depleted K562 cells, we assayed the mRNA expression of heme biosynthesis

pathway genes. We found significant up‐regulation of the rate‐limiting45 enzyme ALAS2 (Fig.

2.3.2E). While depletion of folate increases mRNA expression of heme biosynthesis pathway

components, there was no accompanied up‐regulation of 1C metabolism genes46. The synthesis of

a single heme molecule requires eight molecules of glycine that can be generated from serine


<!-- Page 47 -->


39

through the action of the folate‐dependent enzyme serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) or

imported from exogenous pools. Although serine was underused under low FA conditions, as

expected from folate depletion, glycine levels were still sufficient to support heme synthesis due

to utilization of exogenous glycine46. The increase in total heme was not associated with an

increase in mitochondrial mass or membrane potential, which suggests a utilization of heme

outside of the mitochondrial respiratory complexes46.

Increased heme synthesis is a hallmark of the erythroid differentiation process47. To test

whether folate deprivation induces erythroid differentiation in additional hematopoietic cell lines,

we measured induction of ALAS2 expression in nine hematopoietic cell lines following folate

deprivation. We observed up‐regulation of ALAS2 only in the three erythroid leukemia lines

included in the panel [MEL, K562, and human erythroleukemia (HEL)] and not in cell lines

derived from other lineages (Fig. 2.3.2F). The induction of ALAS2 expression was not correlated

with growth rate in low FA46. In addition, we observed no induction of the nonerythroid heme

synthesis enzyme, ALAS1 46. This supports an erythroid specific role of heme synthesis in folate‐

deprived cells as opposed to a broad up‐regulation of heme synthesis in all leukemia cell lines.

We therefore validated the induction of heme synthesis and the increase in differentiation

markers following mild folate deprivation in two additional erythroid cell lines; the mouse line,

MEL48, and the human line, HEL49. Over 8 days in low FA, K562 cells increase expression of fetal

hemoglobin [found in K562 cells although these are not embryonic‐derived cells50] and

hemoglobin A1 (Fig. 2.3.2G), as well as the erythroid cell surface marker glycophorin A (GlyA)

(Fig. 2.3.2H). Both MEL and HEL increased hemoglobin A1 protein expression (Fig. 2.3.2, I and

K). Despite hemoglobin levels increasing in low FA, these results are not reflecting through

benzidine staining 46. We assayed the erythroid differentiation surface markers Ter119 and GlyA


<!-- Page 48 -->


40

found on MEL and HEL, respectively, following folate deprivation. While no change in GlyA

surface expression was observed in HEL, MEL significantly increased expression of Ter119 (Fig.

2.3.2, J and L). Together, our data reveal induction of erythroid differentiation by mild folate

deprivation.

Our metabolite profiling data of 6‐day folate‐deprived K562 revealed accumulation of

protoporphyrin IX, a metabolite that, together with iron, generates a complete heme molecule33

(Fig. 2.3.2D). This raised the possibility that folate‐deprived K562 suffers from lack of iron due to

increased demand from up‐regulated heme synthesis. However, neither iron supplementation,

either as free iron (Fe2+) or transferrin‐bound iron (Fe2+‐transferrin), nor iron chelation (using

deferoxamine) altered proliferation or differentiation, although these treatments result in the

expected changes in transferrin receptor expression46. These data rule out a role for iron availability

or limitation as a driver of folate deprivation–induced differentiation.

Induction of differentiation in response to mild folate depletion occurs independently of DNA

damage

Because folate deficiency is suggested to cause anemia through DNA damage in erythroid

progenitor cell and this is considered to be the cause of megaloblastic anemia8, 23, 51, we set to

monitor DNA damage in mild folate deprivation (100 nM) in K562 cells. We added lower

concentrations of folate to model more severe folate depletion as controls and included 2000, 100,

50, and 20 nM FA culture conditions for 48 hours. Folate depletion at these doses and timescale

allowed cell proliferation in culture, and we observed no significant impairment in proliferation 46.

We observed a significant depletion of THF in all three low FA concentrations 46, but this has not

yet manifested in a proliferation defect. We also observed a dose‐dependent increase in serine and

decrease in glycine, and accumulation of the purine synthesis intermediates GAR and AICAR 46.

On the other hand, guanosine 5′‐triphosphate (GTP) levels were more stable46. After characterizing

the metabolic impact of these various FA concentrations, we set to test whether erythroid cells

cultured in these FA concentrations suffer from DNA damage. We assessed the level of DNA

damage via phosphorylation of the DNA damage–responsive protein checkpoint kinase 1 (Chk1)

and the level of apoptosis via cleaved caspase III. We found that unlike more severe FA

depletion52, 100 nM dose of FA does not result in increased p‐Chk1/Chk1 ratio or cleaved caspase

III following 6 days of FA depletion in K562 and MEL46. Comparison of 100 nM FA folate

depletion to H2O2 treatment revealed a mild phosphorylation of Chk1, only later than 4 days of

folate deprivation, and no detection of phospho‐H2A histone family member X, S139 (γH2AX) in

folate‐deprived cells46. In addition, immunofluorescence quantification of γH2AX in mild or

severely folate‐deprived cells reveals no significant increase in DNA‐damage following 2 days of

culture, while known inducer of DNA damage, doxorubicin, leads to a significant increase in


<!-- Page 52 -->


44

γH2AX in both K562 and MEL46. These data confirm that mild folate deprivation results in

erythroid differentiation independently of DNA damage. This suggests that DNA damage–induced

stress response or apoptosis is not the cause of the reduced erythroid cell numbers found following

mild folate deprivation.

Purine biosynthesis inhibition is an early event following folate deprivation, and purine

supplementation rescues folate depletion–induced differentiation

FA is directly and indirectly involved in many metabolic reactions, including nucleotide synthesis,

amino acid metabolism, and methylation reactions. Therefore, we asked which metabolic changes

in folate deprived erythroid cells drive differentiation. We addressed this by first mapping the

kinetics of the cellular response to low folate availability; transcriptionally, induction of heme

biosynthesis gene expression in K562 occurs at day 4 following folate deprivation (Fig. 2.3A).

Heme levels were increased following these gene expression changes at day 646. These

transcriptional and metabolic effects followed the depletion of 10‐formyl THF as early as 1 day

following folate depletion (Fig. 2.3B). Metabolically, the purine synthesis pathway46 was the first

pathway to show significant perturbations in both K562 and MEL cells as early as day 2 following

folate deprivation (Fig. 2.3, C and D): At day 2, K562 and MEL cells had 7 and 21 significantly

altered metabolites, respectively, with AICAR, GAR, and ribose‐1‐phosphate (R1P), the only

shared metabolites between the two cell lines. AICAR and GAR are intermediates of the purine

synthesis pathway, and R1P is the byproduct of purine salvage reactions (Fig. 2.3.2B). Although

folate is essential for IMP and deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) synthesis, examination of

nucleotide levels in K562 and MEL showed that while there is a slight reduction in adenosine 5′‐

triphosphate (ATP) and GTP in K562 and MEL over 4 days of FA depletion, no major pyrimidine


<!-- Page 53 -->


45

synthesis inhibition occurs46. Therefore, although pyrimidine synthesis inhibition can be

associated with myeloid leukemia differentiation53, it is not likely to be the metabolic driver of the

erythroid differentiation we observe here. In addition, the ratio of glutathione/oxidized glutathione

does not change significantly, and the reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide

phosphate (NADP+) (NADPH)/NADP and reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide

(oxidized form) (NAD+) (NADH)/NAD ratios are significantly higher in K562 after 8 days in 100

nM FA. These data suggest that folate depletion is not associated with increased reactive oxygen

species (ROS) or redox imbalance46.

Previous studies in erythroleukemia have shown that both purine supplementation54, 55  and

inhibition of purine synthesis56, 57 can induce erythroid differentiation. Therefore, the early

inhibition of purine synthesis led us to hypothesize that perturbation of this pathway drives a stress

response that results in erythroid cell differentiation. To assess this hypothesis, we rescued purine

synthesis by supplementation with inosine (100 μM), a purine salvage intermediate, that enables

purine synthesis while bypassing folate‐dependent de novo synthesis 46. Inosine supplementation

restored the proliferation rate of K562 and MEL cells in low FA 46. There was no effect of inosine

on proliferation in high FA–cultured cells. Inosine supplementation also blocked folate

deprivation–induced differentiation, as observed by the lack of induction of ALAS2 expression

(Fig. 2.3, E and I), the reduction in hemoglobin synthesis (Fig. 2.3, G and K), and the reduction in

the erythroid surface marker Ter119 in MEL cells (Fig. 2.3J). However, GlyA surface expression

was not rescued with inosine in K562 (Fig. 2.3F). In addition, treatment with inosine erased nearly

all the metabolic changes associated with low FA at day 2 in K562 and MEL cells leaving only

FA, serine, and glycine significantly different (Fig. 2.3, H and L). As expected, inosine treatment

rescued de novo purine synthesis defects and nucleotide levels 46. This suggests that neither the

absence of FA nor the accumulation of intracellular serine drives differentiation on their own but

that perturbation of purine synthesis is the driver of folate deprivation–induced differentiation.

These data (Fig. 2.3, H and L) may also indicate that inosine supplementation under low

FA conditions allows limiting pools of folate molecules to be redirected to other nonpurine, folate‐

dependent reactions so that low FA medium supplemented with inosine may permit cells to

maintain all cellular folate–required reactions and avoid the metabolic stress that is otherwise

associated with folate deprivation. Further work will be needed to address this specific question.

purine synthesis pathway 46, occurs early enough to be acting as an inducer of the differentiation

program. AMPK signaling was activated shortly after the elevation in AICAR levels as measured

by the phosphorylation of acetyl‐coA carboxylase (ACC) and Unc‐51‐like autophagy activating

kinase 1 (ULK1), two principle downstream targets of AMPK (Fig. 2.6, A and B)14. In addition,

to induce erythroid differentiation, we applied the pharmacologic AMPK activator GSK62164.

differentiation by genetically targeting both AMPKa1 and AMPKa2 [AMPKa double knockout

In addition to its role in activating AMPK, AICAR can activate PKC65 , and PKC inhibition rescues

activation. We therefore investigated the role of PKC in mediating folate depletion–induced

differentiation. First, we tested the necessity of PKC signaling in folate deprivation–induced

differentiation by inhibiting PKC signaling. We treated K562 and MEL with the PKC inhibitor

GF109203X (GFX), alone or in combination with low FA, SHIN1, or AICAR. We first assessed

the toxicity of the treatment through its impact on cell proliferation. In both K562 and MEL, GFX

alone compromised proliferation over 6 days of treatment 46. As expected, treatment with low FA,

SHIN1, and AICAR impaired proliferation. The addition of PKC inhibition by GFX rescued

AICAR‐induced proliferation effect in K562 and MEL. However, GFX treatment resulted in the

opposite effect in folate‐deprived or SHIN1‐treated cells. The mechanism driving this difference

between the treatments combinations is unclear, but we suspect that this is related to other 1C

metabolism functions and not to the metabolic axis we study here that includes perturbation of 1C

metabolism, purine synthesis inhibition, AICAR up‐regulation, and induction of a differentiation

program. PKC inhibition by GFX mitigated metabolic differentiation in both K562 and MEL, as

reflected by the markers of erythroid differentiation ALAS2 and GlyA/Ter119 (Fig. 2.7, A and B).

in response to low FA, SHIN1, or AICAR treatment (Fig. 2.7C). SHIN1 treatment led to a decrease

in phosphorylated PKC substrates. These data suggest that PKC’s role in differentiation may be

Folate deprivation depletes choline metabolism intermediates, but choline supplementation is

not sufficient to rescue folate depletion–induced differentiation

Our metabolite profiling of K562 and MEL cells treated with low FA, AICAR, and SHIN1

revealed a significant reduction in the choline metabolism pathway, including choline,

glycerophosphocholine (GPC), and phosphocholine46 (Fig. 2.6, H to K). The metabolic association

between choline and folate metabolism stems from a shared reaction: In the methionine cycle, the

folate form 5‐methyl THF is required for the conversion of homocysteine to methionine by the

enzyme Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR). Alternatively, methionine can be

synthesized from homocysteine by the enzyme betaine‐homocysteine S‐methyltransferase

(BHMT) using betaine, instead of 5‐methyl THF, as the methyl donor. Betaine is synthesized from

choline by the enzyme choline dehydrogenase (CHDH) 46. This connection presented two

possibilities: (i) Choline metabolism is up‐regulated in low FA to support the methionine cycle

and maintain cellular methylation, and (ii) the depletion of both FA and choline could lead to

methylation defects and epigenetic reprogramming that induces differentiation. With these

possibilities in mind and coupled with the fact that choline metabolism is essential for murine and

human erythropoiesis66, we verified reduction of metabolites of this pathway in 1C metabolism–

perturbed K562  and MEL 46. To test the role of choline in folate depletion induced differentiation,

we supplemented K562 with choline (500 μM) under 2000 or 100 nM FA conditions.

Supplementation with choline did not alter proliferation or rescued differentiation46, and choline

supplementation increased ALAS2 mRNA expression in low FA compared to low FA alone. These

results suggest that lack of choline is not a sufficient cause of folate deprivation–induced

differentiation.

We next tested whether folate deprivation induces differentiation in primary erythroid progenitor

cells (Fig. 2.8A). For this, we used an ex vivo murine erythroid progenitor differentiation system

61, 67, 68 that allows controlled nutritional and pharmacological perturbations of 1C metabolism in

primary progenitor cells with an established readout of differentiation. We isolated erythroid

progenitors from fetal livers of embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) embryos and purified an enriched

population of erythroid cells primarily composed of the erythroid committed progenitor

This ex vivo differentiation model of erythroid cells can be set up as two phases, expansion and

differentiation, as dictated by the presence or absence of growth factors in the medium. For

addressing our biological question, we focused on culturing cells in the expansion phase to allow

maintenance of undifferentiated progenitor cells, maintained by insulin‐like growth factor–1 (IGF‐

1) and stem cell factor (SCF) that are present in the medium. The differentiation phase, achieved

by removal of growth factors, is less suitable for our study because the strong differentiation drive

is likely to mask any differentiation effect of 1C metabolism inhibition. The optimal commercial

medium commonly used for progenitor expansion [Serum‐Free Expansion Medium II (SFEM II)]

contains supraphysiological levels of folate. We therefore cultured the purified erythroid

population in a custom folate‐depleted RPMI‐based expansion medium that contains additional

growth factors. Notably, erythroid progenitor cells cultured in this custom medium supplemented

with 2000 nM FA proliferate successfully but trend toward an early differentiation phenotype 46.

### 2.3 Discussion

Deprivation of the essential vitamin folate results in megaloblastic anemia in children and

adults70, 71. This disease remains a major health incumbrance in underdeveloped countries72, 73  and

in underserved populations, where nutritional shortage of folate still prevails even in our era of

folate fortification and common supplementation40, 74. Megaloblastic anemia is characterized by

the appearance of big, hemoglobin‐filled erythrocytes75, 76. Early studies have suggested that

folate‐deficient anemia is a result of DNA damage induced apoptosis8, 23. It has been thought that

the absence of folate decreases thymidylate synthesis and, subsequently, the ratio of 3′‐

deoxythymidine 5′‐triphosphate:deoxyuridine triphosphate. As a result, uracil is mis-incorporated

into DNA, induces DNA damage, and leads to increased erythroid apoptosis, which manifests as

anemia. However, although several studies have called into question this mechanism of folate‐

deficient anemia because of lack of molecular evidence for both DNA damage and apoptosis of

erythroid progenitors77, 78, no alternative hypothesis has yet emerged.

Our data indicate that folate deprivation induces a metabolic stress that results in aberrant

differentiation of erythroid cells. Premature differentiation of progenitor cells can result in

insufficient number of cell division cycles that normally precede differentiation and reduced cell

numbers of cells of that lineage (Fig. 8). Our results suggest an etiology to the low cell count of

erythroid cells in megaloblastic anemia and to the unique manifestation of this disease—large,

heme filled cells. We describe here a folate deprivation–induced increase in heme metabolism that

is regulated transcriptionally. While we have not yet identified the upstream signaling cascade that

is driving the transcriptional response to folate deprivation, we postulate that the drop in cellular

folate is being sensed, either directly or through purine levels, leading to signal transduction and

activation of a differentiation program. Our data rule out the involvement of two major signaling


<!-- Page 80 -->


72

pathways that respond to changes in purine levels—the mTORC1 and AMPK pathways—and we

postulate that another signaling cascade bridges the drop in folate availability and activation of the

differentiation program in erythroid cells. Notably, we provide evidence that the signaling pathway

bridging folate availability and activation of erythroid differentiation involves the kinase PKC.

Inhibition of PKC rescues 1C metabolism perturbation–induced differentiation in K562, MEL, and

primary progenitor cells, and its activation induces differentiation in MEL cells. Our results

confirm previous connections between AICAR and PKC34, suggesting an axis between high

AICAR, PKC activation, and induction of the gene expression program that results in erythrocyte

differentiation. Previous studies have presented conflicting views of PKC’s involvement in

erythroid differentiation79, 80, so future work should focus on the context specific regulation of

differentiation by PKC. By mimicking the mild shortage in folate availability of nutritional folate

deprivation and by comprehensive profiling of the metabolic consequences of this mild folate

deprivation in erythroid cells, we identified premature, aberrant differentiation process that can

explain the manifestation of megaloblastic anemia, including low erythroid cell counts and large,

heme‐filled cells. Therefore, our work identifies a molecular etiology for nutritional megaloblastic

anemia and demonstrates that a metabolic stress can alter differentiation dynamics in a clinically

relevant developmental biology model system.

Polar metabolites, folates, and porphyrins were relatively quantified while referencing an in‐house

library of chemical standards and using TraceFinder 4.1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA,

USA), with a 5–part per million mass tolerance. Pooled samples and fractional dilutions were

prepared as quality controls and injected at the beginning and end of each run. Pooled samples

were interspersed throughout the run to control for technical drift in signal quality and for

averaged across samples. Metabolite peak areas were then divided by the resulting factor

(biological normalizer), thus accounting for any global shift in metabolite amounts due to

### 3.1 Abstract

Cells survive by sensing and adapting to factors in their environment. Nutrients in

particular are essential but potentially variable in a cell’s environment, which necessitates a

balance in cell metabolism and can lead the cell towards anabolism or catabolism. In order to

promote survival, cells sometimes limit proliferation in an environment with insufficient

nutrients. Although it is known that a low-nutrient environment (limited amino acids) inhibits the

mTOR pathway and leads to, amongst other changes, protein degradation, cellular autophagy,

and changes in translation (PMID: 37494188; PMID: 28918901; PMID: 26669439), the cellular

response to the deprivation of folate remains mostly unknown. In our efforts to address this gap,

we conducted a genome-wide loss-of-function CRISPR screen to define the genetic

dependencies of folate depletion and uncover the genes and pathways involved in the cellular

adaptation to folate deficiency. This analysis revealed numerous previously unrecognized links

to folate metabolism, including the UFMylation pathway. While pursuing this connection, we

questioned the impact of perturbing 1CM via folate depletion on ribosomal quality control and

translation in the cell.

Using the K562 erythroleukemia cell line, I found potential connections between 1CM

perturbation via folate depletion and changes to ribosomal regulation. The knockout of

UFMylation pathway genes scored higher for survival in folate depleted media compared to WT

cells in our CRISPR screen. Current knowledge of UFMylation closely ties this post-translation

modification to ribosomal regulation in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), but it has not yet been

connected to nutritional deprivation. We subsequently found that there is differential ribosomal

regulation in cells deprived of folate, shown by ribosome sequencing (Riboseq) data. In addition,

through both the CRISPR screen and Riboseq we found evidence of a role of glycosylation genes


<!-- Page 103 -->


39

in the fitness of cells deprived of folate, furthering our hypothesis that cellular adaptation to 1CM

stress may induce changes in ribosomal control.

Together, these data provide insight into the control of cellular adaptation and survival

following interruption of 1CM. The completion of this project will improve our understanding of

the cellular mechanisms used for adaptation to nutrient insufficiency, which is broadly relevant

in the clinical setting, particularly for patients experiencing folate-deficiency-induced anemia,

patients who use methotrexate for cancer or autoimmune disease, and also in the context of the

nutrient-depleted cancer microenvironment.

### 3.2 Introduction

UFMylation

Overview of the UFMylation pathway and its physiological functions

Ubiquitin fold modifier 1 (UFM1) is an 85–amino acid ubiquitin-like protein (UBL) that

is widely expressed across metazoans but absent from fungi, and it has been found to be

indispensable for brain and hematopoietic development in mouse studies using genetic disruption

of the UFMylation pathway1, 2. Similar to ubiquitin and other UBLs, UFM1 is conjugated to lysine

residues on substrate proteins through a three-step enzymatic cascade involving the E1, E2, and

E3 enzymes, encoded by UBA5, UFC1, and UFL1, respectively (Figure 3.1). Removal of UFM1

from its targets is mediated by the UFM1-specific protease UFSP2. The UFM1 E3 ligase, UFL1,

localizes to the cytosolic surface of the ER. It is also known that genes encoding UFMylation

components are transcriptional targets of the unfolded protein response (UPR), and the UFM1

promoter harbors a putative binding site for the ER stress-responsive transcription factor XBP13.

Overall, the UFM1 pathway represents a highly conserved mechanism that coordinates ER

homeostasis with cellular and organismal development.

While the enzymatic framework of UFMylation is well characterized, its physiological

functions remain incompletely understood. In humans, hypomorphic loss-of-function variants in

UFM1, UBA5, or UFSP2 give rise to various pathologies, including leukodystrophy, epileptic

encephalopathy, spinocerebellar ataxia, and skeletal malformations, underscoring the essential role

of UFMylation in the heart, kidneys, brain, liver, and bone marrow2, 4-12. UFMylation has been

closely associated with the regulation of secretory cells involved in the endocrine system by

maintaining ER proteostasis in mice13, 14. Although the UFMylation pathway is not required for

cell viability in vitro, loss of Uba5, Ufl1, or Ddrgk1 in mice causes embryonic lethality


<!-- Page 105 -->


41

accompanied by defective hematopoiesis, while cardiac-specific deletion of Ufl1 results in

cardiomyopathy. Interestingly, both of these phenotypes are associated with elevated ER stress

markers2. Collectively, these findings highlight UFMylation as a vital regulator of tissue

homeostasis whose disruption compromises ER function and organ development.

Although several cellular proteins have been proposed as UFM1 substrates, few have been

conclusively demonstrated to form covalent UFM1 conjugates under physiological conditions or

to account for the cellular and organismal phenotypes observed in UFMylation-deficient states.

Among the limited number of validated substrates, one in particular has provided critical insight

into the biological significance of UFMylation: RPL26.

RPL26 - a primary UFMylation target

It has been reported that the primary target of UFMylation is a single lysine residue on the

ribosomal protein uL24 (also referred to as RPL26), located on ribosomes associated with the

cytoplasmic face of the ER. UFM1 binding enables the recycling of 60S ribosomal subunits

released through ribosome-associated quality control, which facilitates the rescue of stalled

ribosomes during the co-translational translocation of secretory proteins into the ER (Fig. 3.2)15.

Notably, several additional UFMylation substrates have been proposed, but their study as

UFMylation substrates is not yet as comprehensive16.

Rescue of stalled ribosomes by UFMylation

To generate and preserve a functional proteome, all cells employ protein quality control

systems that continuously monitor the proteome, selectively eliminating proteins that fail to attain

or maintain their native three-dimensional structures due to damage, synthesis errors, misfolding,

or defects in oligomeric assembly. Beyond proteome monitoring, protein quality control also

operates at the ribosome through a specialized pathway termed ribosome-associated quality

control. Ribosome stalling during translation elongation can arise from damaged mRNA, depletion

of charged aminoacyl-tRNA pools, or the presence of particular mRNA sequences. In eukaryotes,

a frequent cause of ribosomal stalling occurs during the translation of poly(A) tracts, which leads

to the synthesis of polylysine homopolymers. Such “nonstop” translation can result either from

ribosomes failing to terminate at stop codons or from premature mRNA polyadenylation. Stalled

ribosomes on poly(A) sequences may resume elongation within the same reading frame, through

a process known as readthrough, or in an alternative frameshift. However, if translation does not

resume promptly, the stalled ribosome collides with an upstream ribosome, forming a distinctive

composite interface that recruits ribosome rescue factors17. These factors mediate the degradation


<!-- Page 108 -->


44

of the incomplete nascent peptide and facilitate recycling of the ribosomal subunits. When

translation stalls occur on cytosolic proteins, the resulting arrested polypeptides are efficiently

recognized and ubiquitylated by the canonical ribosome-associated quality control pathway,

subsequently degraded by the 26S proteasome, thereby releasing a rescued 60S ribosomal subunit

capable of re-entering protein synthesis. However, stalls that arise on ribosomes engaged in

cotranslational translocation into the ER generate ER-associated arrested polypeptides, which are

shielded from the cytosolic ubiquitin-proteasome system by the ribosome-translocon junction and

consequently disrupt both protein translocation and ribosome function. Scavone et al. (2023)

demonstrated that UFMylation facilitates the recovery of stalled, ER-associated ribosomes,

allowing their release back into the cytosol for reuse18.

The ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) machinery is required to dislocate arrested

peptides from ribosomes stalled at the ER since the nascent chains are shielded from the cytoplasm

by the ribosome–translocon junction (RTJ)19. When ribosomes collide at the ER, they are separated

by ZNF598 and ASCC3, producing a 60S-AP-tRNA complex in which the partially translocated

nascent chain extends from the ribosomal P-site through the exit tunnel and translocon into the ER

lumen. ZNF598 and ASCC3 are important components of the RQC pathway20, 21. ZNF598 serves

as a sensor that recognizes ribosome collisions and marks them through ubiquitination, while

ASCC3, a helicase within the ASCC complex, facilitates disassembly of the stalled ribosomal

complex. Together, these factors help preserve proteostasis by removing stalled ribosomes and

promoting the degradation of incomplete polypeptides. The stalled ER-associated nascent chain is

recognized by NEMF (nuclear export mediator factor), a central component of the RQC pathway,

which recognizes stalled 60S ribosomal subunits and promotes the ubiquitination and degradation

of incomplete, potentially harmful polypeptides. NEMF adds CAT tails (C-terminal alanine and


<!-- Page 109 -->


45

threonine residues) to the stalled polypeptide, which helps LTN1 access ubiquitination sites to the

ER-anchored peptide, thereby promoting LTN1-dependent ubiquitylation and proteasomal

degradation of the arrested peptide. In yeast, the absence of Ltn1 disrupts extraction of ER-

associated RQC substrates, resulting in nonstop peptides being released into the ER lumen. It was

observed that some ER-anchored peptides enter the lumen spontaneously, and this proportion

increases substantially when RQC or UFMylation pathways are impaired. Thus, ER-associated

nascent chains can backslide into the cytosol through a UFM1-dependent mechanism requiring

RQC factors and ubiquitin-driven ATPases, or can be released into the ER lumen. The likelihood

of each outcome is hypothesized to depend on the timing of the arrested peptide release from the

60S after peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis, ER-AP ubiquitylation, and extraction after ribosomal

disassembly18.

Cellular homeostasis

Cells maintain homeostasis by balancing anabolism and catabolism

All living systems rely on a continuous supply of energy and biosynthetic precursors to

support growth, maintenance, and function. Maintaining the balance between the generation and

use of these resources is fundamental to cellular homeostasis. This balance arises from the

coordinated regulation of two opposing processes: catabolism, which breaks down nutrients to

produce energy and recycle building blocks from proteins and organelles, and anabolism, which

utilizes the energy and building blocks to build macromolecules (Fig. 3.3). The significance of this

interplay is evident when contrasting proliferating cells with those that are in a quiescent state.

Dividing cells remodel their metabolic programs to emphasize anabolic reactions that generate the

proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids needed for cell growth and replication. In

contrast, most differentiated tissues consist of non-dividing cells with a more balanced

metabolism, tuned to sustain energy homeostasis and preserve cellular integrity and function. The

ability to sustain and dynamically regulate the balance between anabolic and catabolic processes

is vital for cell viability, and eukaryotic cells have developed sophisticated mechanisms to

modulate these pathways in response to environmental and physiological changes23.

In multicellular systems, cells must coordinate systemic physiological signals with local

environmental inputs to preserve energy homeostasis and cellular integrity. This regulation is

primarily achieved through secreted molecules, such as hormones and growth factors, that engage

cell surface receptors to trigger signaling pathways governing metabolism. Concurrently, cells

continuously assess internal metabolite concentrations to ensure that nutrient supply matches their

metabolic demands, enabling adjustment of signaling networks even in the absence of extracellular

cues. Recent studies indicate that metabolites do more than reflect cellular metabolic status; they


<!-- Page 112 -->


48

also serve as signaling entities that influence post-translational modifications (including

acetylation, methylation, and glycosylation), thereby modulating the function of signaling

enzymes and transcriptional regulators23. Ultimately, cells maintain energy and functional balance

by integrating signals with internal metabolic feedback. Metabolites themselves act as messengers

that modify proteins and adjust cellular signaling, allowing precise coordination between

metabolism and cellular function.
