Nutrient availability regulates translation

Proliferating cells adopt an anabolic metabolic state to meet the increased demand for

macromolecule synthesis required for cell division. Cancer cells exemplify this adaptation by

rewiring glycolytic flux at multiple regulatory nodes to channel intermediates into biosynthetic

pathways, including the pentose phosphate pathway, serine and glycine biosynthesis, and de novo

nucleotide production. Nucleotides are indispensable for fundamental cellular processes such as

DNA replication, RNA transcription, energy metabolism, glycosylation, and intracellular

signaling. The mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) coordinates nucleotide

biosynthesis with anabolic growth by promoting de novo purine synthesis and stimulating

pyrimidine production through activation of key metabolic enzymes. Reciprocal regulation also

exists between purine availability and mTORC1 activity. Pharmacological depletion of purine

nucleotides with antimetabolites such as methotrexate (MTX) or lometrexol (LTX) strongly

suppresses mTORC1 signaling, underscoring the importance of purines in sustaining mTORC1-

dependent cellular and metabolic functions. Despite their central role in proliferation and growth,

the mechanisms by which cells sense and adapt to fluctuations in intracellular purine levels remain

incompletely understood.

Purine metabolism and its role in cellular homeostasis

Purine nucleotides serve not only as the fundamental components of nucleic acids but also

as precursors for cofactors, signaling molecules, and cellular building blocks. Cellular purine pools

are maintained through a balance between biosynthetic and degradative pathways. Purine

biosynthesis occurs via two main routes, the de novo and salvage pathways. The adjustment of

cells to purine levels has been studied extensively in cancer cells. Cancer cells alter their metabolic


<!-- Page 115 -->


51

networks to satisfy the elevated demand for nucleotides and other macromolecules required for

rapid growth and division. Notably, they exhibit enhanced de novo synthesis of purine

nucleotides24.

Purine nucleotides are central to cellular homeostasis, serving not only as building blocks

for DNA and RNA but also as key regulators of energy balance and signaling. Cells respond to

purine depletion by activating coordinated metabolic and stress-response pathways that limit

proliferation and restore homeostasis25. Reduced availability of purine nucleotides, such as ATP

and GTP, disrupts DNA and RNA synthesis and imposes replication stress, particularly in rapidly

dividing cells26, 27. As a result of impaired nucleic acid synthesis, the accumulation of upstream

intermediates such as AICAR can activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)28. Activated

AMPK suppresses anabolic processes, including nucleotide and protein synthesis, in part through

inhibition of mTORC1, promoting catabolic pathways and leading to a coordinated reduction in

anabolic activity and cell proliferation25. In parallel, cells may alter gene expression and cell cycle

progression, often leading to S-phase arrest or slowed proliferation. Together, these responses

reflect an integrated effort to couple nucleotide availability with growth control, ensuring that

growth, division, and biosynthesis are tightly coupled to metabolic capacity.

As mentioned in the thesis introduction, mTORC1 is linked to translation through multiple

mechanisms. This includes regulation of cell size through mTOR phosphorylation of S6K, which

is essential to the translational control of TOP mRNAs, a class of transcripts that encode essential

translational machinery, namely ribosomal proteins, and elongation factors29, 30 (Fig. 3.4). This

process is nutrient and growth factor sensitive, regulated by the Raptor subunit within the

mTORC1 complex31. In fact, loss or repression of TOP mRNAs, triggered by mTORC1 signaling

inhibition during nutrient or oxygen stress, can cause ribosomal stalling. This occurs via la-related


<!-- Page 116 -->


52

protein 1 (LARP1), which functions as a key regulator of translation downstream of the nutrient-

sensing kinase complex mTORC1, where it acts to repress the translation of TOP mRNAs. It

mediates this effect by binding both the mRNA cap structure and the adjacent 5′TOP motif, thereby

preventing association of the cap-binding protein eIF4E with these transcripts. Moreover, it has

been reported that LARP1 participates in a complex for recruitment to stalled ribosomes in nutrient

stress conditions32 (Fig. 3.4). Taken together, mTORC1 is closely connected to the regulation of

ribosome function and translation itself under conditions of nutrient depletion, and many aspects

of this relationship remain to be fully understood.

mTOR senses nutrients, including purines

mTORC1 serves as a key metabolic hub that integrates signals from nutrients and growth

factors to regulate anabolic pathways, including the synthesis of proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids.

Hoxhaj et al. (2017) demonstrated that mTORC1 activity is responsive to purine depletion. They

found that the loss of intracellular purines, but not pyrimidines, suppresses mTORC1 signaling,

while replenishment of adenine nucleotides through purine nucleobase or nucleoside

supplementation restores its activity. These findings reveal that mTORC1 senses purine

availability in a manner analogous to amino acid sensing, thereby aligning nucleotide abundance

with the biosynthesis of macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids33.

Folate depletion and mTOR activity

Given the essential role of folate in normal physiology and its association with diverse

diseases, it has been proposed that restricted fetal growth in the context of low maternal folate

arises from impaired trophoblast mTOR folate sensing, leading to mTORC1/2 inhibition and


<!-- Page 117 -->


53

reduced placental amino acid transport34. In their Journal of Physiology 2017 paper, Rosario et al.

(Jansson lab) suggest that mTOR acts as a folate sensor in primary human trophoblast (PHT) cells,

in a process requiring both mTORC1 and mTORC2 as well as the proton-coupled folate

transporter35. They postulate that folate directly regulates trophoblast function. Furthermore, they

suggested that given mTOR’s role in promoting placental amino acid transport and mitochondrial

activity, mTOR-mediated folate sensing may represent a critical link between maternal folate

status and fetal growth. However, these studies were performed in trophoblasts, cells that comprise

the outer layer of the blastocyst that ultimately helps to mediate maternal-fetal nutrient exchange,

and which require and respond in a cell-specific manner to environmental nutrient levels.

Additionally, they cultured the PHT cells for 24, 48, 72 or 90 hours in folate deficient media to

study the effect on mTOR. mTORC1 activity is known to respond rapidly to changes in nutrients,

due to the rapid turnover of its repressors, within minutes to hours36, 37. Due to the timing used, the

results reported are difficult to disentangle purine depletion sensing from potential folate sensing.

Adjustments to nutrient changes promotes cell survival

Nutrient-sensing mechanisms are critical for preserving cellular homeostasis by

coordinating downstream metabolic activities. For instance, activation of AMPK enhances

catabolic pathways that generate ATP while simultaneously inhibiting energy-consuming anabolic

processes. Conversely, when nutrients are abundant, activation of mTORC1 stimulates anabolic

pathways, including protein synthesis, to supply the macromolecular components necessary for

cell growth and proliferation. In other words, nutrient sufficiency induces anabolism38.

The stress-responsive catabolic process known as autophagy has evolved in cells and can

be activated in response to nutrient deprivation. In this pathway, non-essential or damaged cellular


<!-- Page 118 -->


54

components are delivered to lysosomes for degradation, and the resulting breakdown products are

recycled to support essential biosynthetic pathways or to generate energy. Additionally, autophagy

can selectively target various intracellular nutrient reserves, allowing for the recycling of a wide

range of metabolites and energy sources, including amino acids, nucleotides, lipids, and

carbohydrates39. However, catabolic processes are not the sole cellular response to nutrient

deprivation. In addition to activating these catabolic processes, the cell can also respond by

inhibiting anabolism. When cells have sufficient nutrients, they are activating translation and

transcription. When they have fewer nutrients, they begin to turn down and turn off transcription.

Additionally, both the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) and the unfolded protein

response (UPR) are catabolic processes that can be induced or dynamically regulated during

nutrient deficiency as a cellular stress response to maintain homeostasis40. Ubiquitination is a

common post-translational modification best known for marking proteins for degradation through

the UPS. The addition and removal of ubiquitin molecules alter the stability and activity of

substrate proteins, thereby influencing their turnover and functional state. The UPS is integral to

numerous cellular processes, including cell division, programmed cell death, autophagy,

endocytosis, DNA repair, and immune regulation41. The UPR occurs at the ER. When cells

experience stress conditions such as elevated reactive oxygen species, ATP depletion, nutrient

deficiency, or protein mutations, normal ER function is disrupted, leading to the accumulation of

misfolded or unfolded proteins. In response, the UPR is activated to restore cellular homeostasis

by reducing protein synthesis, increasing the production of molecular chaperones that facilitate

protein folding, and, if the stress persists, initiating programmed cell death42.

In Thoreen et al. it was reported that mTORC1 regulates mRNA translation. When

mTORC1 is inactive, 4E-BPs associate with eIF4E and prevent its interaction with eIF4G1,


<!-- Page 119 -->


55

thereby disrupting assembly of the eIF4F complex and weakening eIF4E’s affinity for the mRNA

cap. Consequently, TOP and TOP-like mRNAs, which rely on stable cap-binding for efficient

translation, lose association with eIF4E and undergo selective translational repression.

Consistently, pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1 with Torin 1 or depletion of eIF4G1

recapitulates this effect, demonstrating that eIF4G1 is required to maintain eIF4E binding to the

cap structure of TOP mRNAs43.

As mentioned, cells adapt to environmental changes and stress by coordinating gene

expression networks that conserve energy and resources, a process that is largely mediated through

mTOR-dependent suppression of protein synthesis. Messenger RNAs containing a 5′ TOP motif,

which are responsible for encoding key components of the protein synthesis machinery, are major

targets of mTORC1-mediated translational regulation. The 5′ TOP motif is a cis-regulatory RNA

element located immediately downstream of the 5’ 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap, characterized

by an invariant cytidine at the first position followed by a continuous stretch of approximately 4

to 15 pyrimidines. Through this mechanism, translation of TOP mRNAs is controlled to

synchronize overall protein synthesis with the production of ribosomal proteins and other factors

essential for ribosome biogenesis44.

CRISPR-Cas9 screen reveals that knockout of UFMylation pathway genes improve cellular

Functional genomics identify essential genes following 1CM perturbation

K562 cells are an immortalized human erythroleukemia cell line derived from a patient

with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). K562 cells are from a folate-deprivation sensitive

erythroid lineage, therefore relevant for studies of folate insufficiency. These non-adherent cells

are cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS). This

media contains 2,000nM folic acid. We found that reducing folic acid content to 100 nM provides

a mild folate stress that allows the cells to survive while also allowing us to study the effects of

folate depletion (refer to Ch. 2 Fig. 1a). To identify genes important or detrimental for cell survival

following folate depletion, we performed a loss-of-function CRISPR/Cas9-based genome-wide

screen (Fig. 3.5a). We performed the CRISPR-Cas9 based screen in K562 cells, an

erythroleukemia cell line. K562 cells are derived from a patient with chronic myelogenous

leukemia and are from the folate-deprivation sensitive erythroid lineage, therefore relevant for

studies of folate insufficiency.

We generated lentivirus using a whole genome sgRNA library targeting ~18,000 genes

with 10 guides per gene to infect the K562 cells. After puromycin selection and recovery, we

divided the cells into dialyzed RPMI media supplemented with 2,000 nM or 100 nM folic and

cultured for 14 population doublings before sequencing. Once the sgRNA reads were calculated,

we determined the log2 fold-change in guide abundance between 2,000 and 100 nM folic acid


<!-- Page 122 -->


58

conditions to the initial input sample after 14 doublings. We then used the difference between the

log2 fold-change for the 2,000 and 100 nM conditions to calculate the CRISPR score.

Differential gene essentiality in folate deplete conditions

Our genome-wide loss of function CRISPR screen revealed genes that are differentially

essential for cell growth in conditions of mild folate deprivation. Some of the hits were anticipated,

and supported by previously published data, including SLC19A1 (Solute Carrier Family 19

Member 1), QDPR (quinonoid dihydropteridine reductase), MTHFS (5,10-

methenyltetrahydrofolate synthetase), and ABCC2 (ATP-binding cassette subfamily C member 2)

(Fig. 3.5b). SLC19A1is a transmembrane protein that acts as the primary importer of folates and

the chemotherapy agent methotrexate into cells46. QDPR reduces quinonoid-dihydrobiopterin back

to active tetrahydrobiopterin, necessary for enzymes involved in aromatic amino acid metabolism

and nitric oxide biology47. MTHFS is the enzyme that helps convert 5-formyl-THF into 5,10-

methenyl-THF, allowing folate to re-enter the active 1C pool48, 49. Knockout of SLC19A1, QDPR,

or MTHFS would be expected to reduce proliferation more strongly under low-folate conditions

since each of these genes supports a different step in maintaining usable intracellular folate and

one-carbon flux. Extracellular folate was limited, thus loss of any factor that helps import,

regenerate, or channel folate cofactors makes nucleotide synthesis and cellular fitness more

difficult to sustain. ABCC2 is an ATP-dependent efflux transporter that removes folates, folate

derivatives, and antifolates like methotrexate (MTX) from cells50. Knockout of ABCC2 may be

expected to improve cellular fitness under conditions where extracellular folate is limited, since

greater intracellular retention of folate would help sustain 1CM and nucleotide synthesis.

UFMylation genes are coessential with genes related to ribosomal regulation

To explore the potential mechanisms involved in the survival of the UFMylation KO cells

from the screen, I made a co-essentiality map using DEPMAP scores. Co-essentiality scores are

calculated by comparing the essentiality profiles of different genes across a panel of cell lines or

conditions. A high positive co-essentiality score suggests that if one gene is essential in a particular

cell line, the other gene is also likely to be essential in that same cell line. I annotated the genes

co-essential with UFM1 by cross-comparing with the GSEA Hallmark gene lists for these

categories (Fig. 3.7a, b). There is a published co-essentiality map from the Kopito Lab, however,

we decided to expand our parameters slightly to capture other potential connections not shown in

their map15. In fact, this allowed us to capture many glycosylation pathway genes in addition to

genes related to ribosomal biogenesis and maturation (Fig. 3.7 b).

SBDS (Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome protein) plays a key role in late-stage

maturation of the 60S large ribosomal subunit, particularly in releasing eIF6 to allow formation of

functional 80S ribosomes. EFL1 (Elongation Factor-Like GTPase 1) works together with SBDS

as a GTPase to drive the removal of eIF6 from the 60S subunit, a critical step in producing

translation-competent ribosomes52. DNAJC21 is a co-chaperone (Hsp40 family) involved in early

steps of ribosome biogenesis, particularly in 60S subunit assembly and processing53. Interestingly,

these genes function in the assembly and maturation of the 60S ribosomal subunit and are required

for the formation of translation-competent ribosomes.

Furthermore, we found interesting connections to glycosylation genes in our map. These genes

are involved in protein glycosylation, specifically in the synthesis and utilization of dolichol-linked

sugar donors used for N-linked glycosylation in the ER. DPM1 and DPM3 are part of the dolichol-

phosphate mannose (DPM) synthase complex. They produce dolichol-phosphate-mannose (Dol-


<!-- Page 128 -->


64

P-Man), a molecule that is a key mannose donor used essential for N-linked glycosylation, O-

mannosylation, and GPI anchor synthesis54. MPDU1 (Mannose-P-Dolichol Utilization Defect 1)

is a protein required for proper use and flipping of dolichol-linked sugars across the ER membrane

and ensures mannose donors are available in the correct location for glycosylation to occur55, 56.

The ALG (Asparagine-Linked Glycosylation) genes we noted in the map are a family of enzymes

that sequentially build the lipid-linked oligosaccharide (LLO) on dolichol so it can then be

transferred to proteins during N-linked glycosylation57. In short, DPM1, DPM3, MPDU1, and

ALG genes encode components of the ER glycosylation machinery, where they function in the

synthesis, utilization, and assembly of dolichol-linked oligosaccharides required for N-linked

glycosylation.

In sum, the coessentiality mapping connected our screen results to ribosomes and the ER

via ribosome biogenesis-related and glycosylation genes. These results encouraged our curiosity

regarding the role of UFMylation in the cellular response to low folate. We hypothesized that there

may be a role of UFMylation in ribosomal regulation at the ER. This also led us to more broadly

question the cellular response to folate deprivation at the ribosomal level.

UFMylation ties to ribosomal biology

Although many binding substrates of UFMylation have been reported, the most highly

investigated is RPL26 (also referred to as ul24)3. RPL26 serves as the primary UFMylation

substrate on the 60S ribosomal subunit, where it becomes modified during ribosome stalling at the

ER15, 22. It is reported that RPL26 is UFMylated by one or multiple UFM1 proteins3.

Given the strong enrichment of UFMylation pathway genes in our screen, along with their

coessentiality with ribosome-associated genes, we hypothesized that UFMylation may help

regulate the balance between anabolic and catabolic processes in response to 1CM disruption

caused by folate depletion. In this context, folate depletion impairs de novo purine synthesis,

resulting in reduced ATP and GTP levels, accumulation of intermediates such as AICAR, and

compromised DNA and RNA synthesis. In this nutrient-limited environment, ribosome stalling

may serve as an adaptive, protective response that preserves cellular fitness by slowing growth.

UFMylation, which has been implicated in rescuing stalled ribosomes, could counteract this

protective stalling by promoting ribosome recycling and translation resumption. While this may

temporarily support continued growth, it may also exacerbate cellular stress and contribute to

decreased viability, ultimately shifting cells toward cell death.

To investigate this, we first predicted that we may see changes in UFMylation protein

levels, or changes in UFMylation target binding, including RPL26 binding, as a response to folate

deprivation. However, we found neither noticeable changes in UFMylation protein levels (9.1 kD)

nor UFMylation target binding levels (above 9.1 kD) using western blotting on cells cultured in

100nM FA media over 6 days (Fig. 3.9a). When we applied RPL26 antibody to these lysates, we

detected consistent levels of RPL26 at the predicted UFMylated molecular weights, with no


<!-- Page 133 -->


69

perceived change in response to folate availability (Fig. 3.9b). However, it is possible that

UFMylation binds other target proteins, despite not being as well described at RPL2659.

To continue investigating the target binding partners of UFM1, we performed

immunoprecipitation (IP) experiments using cellular lysates of K562 cells in folate replete and

deplete conditions. The Kopito Lab at Stanford University performs cellular fractionation for a

majority of their western blots of UFM1, and as the interaction between UFM1 and RPL26 occurs

at the ER, we too added this additional step to improve our results.

Unexpectedly, we found that RPL26 does not appear to be UFMylated in our system, as

we saw a clear band of ~17kDa of unbound RPL26 in our input and RPL26 IP fraction, but no

visible bands at 27 or 37kDa (Fig. 3.9c). Furthermore, we did not see UFM1 in the RPL26 fraction,

even at a high exposure time (Fig. 3.9d). Next, we compared the cytosolic vs. membrane fractions

of cells cultured in folate replete and deplete media and found no visible difference between RPL26

levels (Fig. 3.9e). These data provide evidence that there is no differential binding of RPL26 by

UFMylation during folate depletion in K562 cells, RPL26 and UFM1 levels do not appear to

change in folate deplete conditions over 6 days, and lastly that UFMylation of other potential

substrates is likely not occurring at the ER. Future experiments to determine the bindings partners

of UFM1 in our system may include mass-spectrometry for proteomics.

As UFMylation is not binding RPL26 in our system, it is possible that UFMylation KO

leads to increased cellular fitness in a low folate environment via unknown binding partners or a

yet undescribed mechanism. More broadly, many questions remain regarding cellular response

and fitness during 1CM perturbation.

Ribosome dynamics during 1CM perturbation

Our investigation of cellular responses to 1CM disruption through folate depletion raised several

questions about how cells adapt to changes in nutrient availability, particularly through

mechanisms involving ribosomal regulation. To elucidate this topic, we performed ribosome

profiling on K562 cells cultured in low FA media (100nM) for 0, 4, or 6 days.

For validation of our experiment, we first assessed the TOP mRNAs, as they are sensitive to

nutrient availability, especially when the mTORC1 signaling pathway is affected. As our CRISPR

stress, mTORC1 is inhibited and the translation of TOP mRNAs should drop sharply, even if the

total RNA levels don't change dramatically60. Therefore, in our data sets, we predict major

H3C12, H3C10, H3C1, H4C8). This is an interesting result as well, as histone regulation in

response to 1CM perturbation has been shown in the literature, mainly in the context of epigenetic

regulation, however, not at the level of transcription. For instance, histone methylation occurs

through SAM, which adds methyl groups to histones, such as H3K4me3 (active transcription) and

H3K27me3 (transcriptional repression of the chromatin)64.

### 3.4 Discussion

Mechanism for improved fitness of UFMylation gene KO K562 cells in low folate remains

unidentified

RPL26 is a UFMylation target on the 60s ribosome, where it is targeted by UFMylation

machinery during ribosomal stalling (Figure 3.2). As cellular stress, particularly nutrient stress,

can lead to ribosomal stalling65, we hypothesized that we would see increased UFMylation of

RPL26 in cells deprived of folate. This hypothesis aligns with the idea that increased anabolic

activity can reduce cellular fitness, whereas suppressing anabolism can enhance fitness under

nutrient-poor conditions. To describe in detail, we hypothesized that cell nutrient stress leads to

increased ribosomal stalling, leading to UFMylation of the stalled 60s ribosomes at RPL26 to

increase ribosomal recycling, allowing for increased translation, thereby increasing cellular

anabolism, resulting in a reduction in cell fitness in nutrient poor environment. However, we did

not see any changes in free RPL26 or free UFM1 levels, or of the UFMylation of RPL26 when

cells are cultured in low folate media (Fig. 3.9). Therefore, it is possible that UFMylation is driving

a different, unknown mechanism in the cell that leads to the improved cellular fitness we found in

the CRISPR screen KO cells during folate deprivation (Figure 3.5).

Despite this, our hypothesis remains that the unknown mechanism of UFMylation

contributes to cellular anabolism, and this is detrimental when 1CM is perturbed, as cellular fitness

during 1CM perturbation increases in KOs of the UFMylation pathway. To further explore this

angle, we could perform a LC-MS proteomics experiment to identify the binding partners of

UFMylation enzymes during folate- replete and deplete conditions. Additionally, we could

measure the impact of 1CM perturbation on ribosomal stalling in our cell system.


<!-- Page 141 -->


77

mTORC1 regulation occurs in response to folate depletion

Through our CRISPR and preliminary Ribo-seq results, we have evidence that folate

deprivation is sensed by mTOR.  This suggests that perturbations in one-carbon metabolism via

folate depletion are integrated into the canonical nutrient-sensing pathways that regulate

translation and cell growth. Consequently, reduced folate sensing through mTOR may regulate

ribosome activity, aligning protein synthesis with metabolic capacity under nutrient-limited

conditions.

Glycosylation is tied to 1CM perturbation

We found ties to glycosylation throughout this project. We found that UFMylation genes

are coessential with glycosylation genes via Depmap analysis, and additionally we found in

preliminary results that the translation of a glycosylation gene, GALNT5, is upregulated after

folate depletion.

In the context of nutrient depletion, reduced flux through the HBP can limit glycosylation,

leading to accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER and activation of the UPR66. This has

direct consequences for ribosomes and translation. Cells can respond to ER stress and nutrient

limitation by downregulating global protein synthesis to conserve resources and prevent further

accumulation of improperly processed proteins- shifting the cell towards catabolism. However, we

are seeing the inverse result since GALNT5 is upregulated, leaving an open question. The

upregulation of GALNT5 during folate stress may suggest that the cell may be regulating towards

improved glycosylation under stress, not towards catabolism. To further explore this topic, we

could perform some glycomics experiments of K562 cultured in folate -replete and -deplete media

to identify changes in regulation of glycosylation during folate deprivation.


<!-- Page 142 -->


78

Future experiments

For the UFM1 single-cell KOs, we should firstly perform a qPCR to assess UFM1 mRNA

levels to validate the KOs. We can then also evaluate UPR and ER stress in the single-cell clones

grown in folate replete and deplete conditions. This may result in an interesting connection

between UFMylation and stress response mechanisms to help us elucidate how UFMylation is

regulating cellular fitness in low folate conditions. We can also perform LC/MS with these cells

to assess whether there is differential regulation of purine metabolism or other metabolic

differences in the UFM1 KOs contributing to increased cell fitness. Lastly, we should also finalize

the Ribo-seq experiments using the paired samples to be able to completely evaluate the changes

to transcription in K562 cells during folate depletion.

Some of our unanswered questions remain: We want to know what is ufmylated in our model and

how it impacts fitness in high and low folate. We want to elucidate how ribosomal regulation is

changing during 1CM perturbation. We want to investigate how glycosylation is impacted by high

and low folate in K562 cells.

### 3.5 Methods

Cell Lines

K562 cell lines were grown in RPMI 1640 Medium supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum

and 1 % penicillin-streptomycin. All cells were maintained at 37°C with 5 % CO2.

Cell Culture Experiments

For the cell culture experiments the media was switched to folate-free RPMI (ffRPMI) + 2,000

nM FA a day before the actual start of the experiment. The cells were seeded at a density of 100,000

cells per mL in the indicated media. After 2-4 days the cells were counted (as indicated) and

reseeded at a density of 100,000 cells per mL or collected.

Western blot

Cells were counted and 1-1.5 mL of the cell suspension was collected and centrifuged for 4 min at

200 x g. Media was aspirated and the cells were resuspended in RIPA buffer (100 μL RIPA buffer

per 1 x 106 cells). Cells were incubated on ice for 30 min to lyse and were then centrifuged for 10

min at 4°C at 10,000 x g. Supernatant containing the protein was collected and protein

concentration was determined using Pierce BCA protein assay kit. Protein mixes were prepared

by adding 20 μL Tris-Glycine Sample Buffer (2x) and 4 μL 500 mM DTT to 20 μg protein. Protein

mix was filled up to a final volume of 40 μL with H2O. For protein samples containing less than

1.25 μg/μL protein, 5x SDS-Page protein loading buffer (Reducing) was used instead of the 2x

Tris-Glycine Sample Buffer and DTT. Therefore 20 μg protein were mixed with 8 μL 5x loading

buffer and was filled up to a final volume of 40 μL with H2O. Samples were incubated at 85°C for

2 min prior to loading. For the SDS-PAGE, if not indicated otherwise, a 10-20% gel was placed

into a running chamber and 1x Tris-Glycine running Buffer was added. 35-40 μL of the protein


<!-- Page 144 -->


80

mix and 5 μL of pre-stained protein ladder was loaded on the gel. The gel was run at a constant

voltage of 125V. For the transfer, a wet transfer protocol was used. The PVDF membrane was

activated by incubating for 30 sec in 100% methanol before use. The protein transfer was run at a

constant voltage of 20V for 1.25-1.5 h on ice. After the transfer the membrane was blocked for 1

h in 5% milk in TBST. The membrane was then cut into sections containing the protein of interest

and incubated with the respective primary antibody in HIKARI solution 1 over night while shaking

at 4 °C. The next day the membrane sections were washed trice with TBST for 5 min each.

Membrane sections were then incubated with HPR (horseradish peroxidase) conjugated secondary

antibody (1:10,000) in 5% milk in TBST for 1 h at room temperature while shaking. Afterwards,

the membranes were washed again trice with TBST for 5 min at room temperature while shaking.

The membranes were then incubated for 1 min with Pierce ECL western blotting substrate and

placed into a X-ray film cassette. Images were acquired by developing X-ray films or using a

ChemiDoc.

ER Membrane Fractionation

Cell fractionation Triton X-100 (TX-100) soluble and insoluble fractions were isolated from 2x106

K562 cells by resuspending a PBS-washed cell pellet in 200 mL of 1% TX-100 solubilization

buffer (1% TX-100, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 20 mM N-

ethylmaleimide, 1 mM PMSF, Roche protease inhibitor cocktail). Lysates were rotated at 4C for

20 min and then cleared by centrifuging at 20,000 xg and 4C for 20 min. The TX-100 soluble

supernatant was collected and the TX-100 insoluble pellet was washed three times with 300 mL

of 1% TX-100 solubilization buffer. The pellet was solubilized by sonicating in 200 mL of 1%

SDS solubilization buffer (1% SDS, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 20


<!-- Page 145 -->


81

mM N-ethylmaleimide, 1 mM PMSF, Roche protease inhibitor cocktail) and cleared by

centrifuging at 20,000 xg and 18C for 20 min. Equal volumes of 1% TX100 soluble and insoluble

fractions were analyzed by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting.

Immunoprecipitation

HCT116 cell pellets were briefly thawed at 37 °C and immediately placed on ice. Cells were lysed

in 1× MCLB buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40) supplemented with protease

inhibitors and 1 mM DTT, followed by incubation at 4 °C with rotation for 20 min. Lysates were

clarified by centrifugation at 16,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C. A fraction of the lysate was reserved

for input analysis, and the remaining supernatant was incubated with anti-HA agarose beads

(Sigma) for 2–4 h at 4 °C with rotation. Beads were washed four times with MCLB buffer,

followed by two additional washes in detergent-free buffer (PBS or Tris/NaCl). Bound proteins

were eluted using HA peptide (250 µg/mL) in PBS or Tris/NaCl buffer at 37 °C with gentle

shaking. Eluates were collected by centrifugation, subjected to a second elution, pooled, and stored

at −20 °C for downstream analysis.

Antibodies

Anti-RPL26 Ribosomal Protein L26 (D8F6) rabbit (Cell signaling Cat# 5400S); Anti-UFM1,

rabbit (Abcam Cat# ab109305); Anti-vinculin (E1E9V) XP® rabbit (Cell signaling Cat# 13901)

qPCR

For the RNA extraction cells 2 x 106 were pelleted and the media was aspirated. Then 200 μL of

RNAzol was added to each cell pellet on ice and homogenized. Afterwards 80 μL of H2O was

added to each sample and mixed by vortexing. The samples were incubated on ice for 10 min,


<!-- Page 146 -->


82

centrifuged for 15 min at 4°C and 12,000 x g and 250 μL of supernatant was then transferred into

a new tube. To the supernatant 250 μL of 100 % isopropanol was added and the samples were

incubated again for 10 min on ice. The samples were centrifuged again for 10 min at 4°C and

12,000 x g. The supernatant was aspirated and 150 μL of 75 % Ethanol was added to the samples.

The samples were centrifuged for 3 min at 4°C and 4,000 x g and the supernatant was aspirated

again. The samples were again washed with 150 μL of 75 % Ethanol and the pellet was then

resuspended in 20 μL H2O. The RNA concentration was determined by using Nanodrop. For the

reverse transcription 1 μg of RNA was diluted in H2O to a total volume of 16 μL. To the 16 μL of

RNA 4 μL of LunaScript RT SuperMix was added. The PCR cycle was run.The cDNA was stored

at -20°C.For the quantitative PCR, the cDNA was diluted 1:20 by adding 180 μL of nuclease-free

H2O to the 20 μL of cDNA mix. Primer mixes were prepared by adding 5 μL of forward and 5 μL

of reverse primer (100 μM, final concentration 5 μM) to 90 μL H2O. Then sample master mixes

were prepared containing 1 μL of cDNA and 3 μL of H2O times the number of genes analyzed (in

triplicates). Then the primer master mixes were prepared containing 5 μL SYBR (2x) and 1 μL of

primer mix times the number of samples (in triplicates). The plate was loaded and the PCR was

run.

RiboSeq prep

Ribosome profiling preparation (day prior to experiment): A TLA120.2 rotor ultracentrifuge was

reserved in advance, and tube balancing was planned prior to use. All required reagents and

materials, including dry ice, were prepared ahead of the experiment. A 34% sucrose cushion was

freshly prepared by diluting 50% sucrose in 1× sucrose gradient buffer (SGB). Stock solutions of

EGTA (100 mM, pH 8.0) and EDTA (0.5 mM, pH 8.0) were prepared or verified prior to use.


<!-- Page 147 -->


83

Polysome lysis buffer (4× PLB; 80 mM Tris pH 7.4, 20 mM MgCl₂, 600 mM NaCl, 4% Triton X-

100) was prepared in advance and stored at 4 °C. All components required for downstream steps

were confirmed to be available. For RNA fragment separation, 15% TBE-urea polyacrylamide

gels were prepared using 29:1 acrylamide/bis-acrylamide. Gel solutions were pre-mixed, heated

to dissolve urea, and brought to final volume prior to casting. Immediately before casting,

ammonium persulfate (APS) and TEMED were added to initiate polymerization.

Ribosome profiling:  All steps were performed on ice or at 4 °C unless otherwise indicated. Cells

were treated with cycloheximide (100 µg/mL, 15 min, 37 °C), washed with ice-cold PBS

containing cycloheximide, and lysed in polysome lysis buffer supplemented with detergents,

RNase inhibitors, DNase I, protease inhibitors, and DTT. Lysates were clarified by centrifugation,

and RNA concentration was measured. A fraction of total RNA was reserved for RNA-seq.

Clarified lysates were subjected to micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion (20 min, 25 °C) to

generate ribosome-protected fragments, and the reaction was quenched with EGTA. Digested

lysates were layered onto a 34% sucrose cushion and ultracentrifuged (TLA120.2 rotor, 111,000

rpm, 1 h, 4 °C) to pellet ribosomes. Ribosome pellets were resuspended in RNA lysis buffer, and

RNA was extracted using a commercial kit. RNA fragments were separated on 15% TBE-urea

polyacrylamide gels, and ribosome-protected fragments (26–34 nt) were excised based on size

markers. RNA was eluted from gel slices, precipitated, and resuspended in nuclease-free water.

Extracted RNA was subjected to end repair, including dephosphorylation and phosphorylation,

followed by cleanup using a column-based purification kit. Purified RNA was used for

downstream library preparation and sequencing. One portion of sample allotted for Ribo-seq and

other portion for RNA-seq. RiboSeq was performed by Daphna Nachmani Lab. The RNASeq was

performed through Azenta.

### 4.1 Discussion

Folate deficiency leads to megaloblastic anemia in both children and adults. This condition

continues to pose a substantial health burden in developing countries, and in underserved

populations, where folate insufficiency persists despite widespread food fortification and routine

supplementation.

A new etiology for folate-deficiency induced megaloblastic anemia

Folate deficiency has been proposed to impair thymidylate synthesis, thereby altering the

dTTP:dUTP ratio1. This imbalance is thought to promote uracil incorporation into DNA, leading

to DNA damage and increased apoptosis of erythroid precursors, ultimately resulting in anemia2.

However, this model has been challenged due to limited molecular evidence for DNA damage or

apoptosis in erythroid progenitors, and no widely accepted alternative mechanism.

Folate deprivation induces metabolic stress that disrupts erythroid differentiation, driving

premature maturation of progenitor cells and reducing their proliferative capacity. This premature

differentiation of progenitor cells limits the number of cell divisions that normally occur before

maturation, resulting in a reduced number of cells within that lineage. We also found that folate

deprivation leads to a transcriptionally regulated increase in cellular heme metabolism. Our results

suggest an etiology that accounts for the decreased erythroid cell numbers and the enlarged,

hemoglobin-rich cells characteristic of megaloblastic anemia. We propose that folate deprivation

is sensed by the cell, activating an erythroid differentiation program through a yet undefined

upstream mechanism. We found that PKC inhibition rescues the differentiation phenotype,

suggesting a possible role in this signaling cascade. Our work also confirmed previously reported

link between AICAR accumulation and PKC signaling, showing a functional connection during


<!-- Page 158 -->


94

differentiation. Through modeling mild folate deficiency in erythroid cells in culture, and profiling

the metabolic consequences, we identified premature and aberrant erythroid differentiation as a

potential mechanistic basis for nutritional megaloblastic anemia.

1CM and nutrient sensing

1CM is a highly conserved metabolic pathway which plays a pivotal role in coupling

nutrient status to gene expression3. Modulation of the translational machinery provides cells with

a rapid mechanism to adjust protein expression in response to environmental factors such as

nutrient availability4. Positioned at the intersection of nucleotide and amino acid metabolism,

translation is directly influenced by 1CM, making this pathway a central regulator of cellular

adaptability and fitness5.

In Ch. 3, we aimed to link folate deprivation induced 1CM-pertubation (inhibited

nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis) with the regulation of the ribosome. We found that

culturing K562 cells in folate-deplete media perturbs 1CM metabolism, leading to changes in

purine synthesis (Ch. 2), and downstream to potential changes in ribosomes and translation (Ch.

3). We found that KO of mTORC1 genes affects cellular fitness in K562 cells cultured in low-

folate media via our CRISPR screen. This supports a connection between 1CM perturbation via

folate depletion and mTORC1 mediated adaptation of the cell. We also found that changes to

translation occurred in genes related to glycosylation, known to have a role in ribosomal

regulation, and histones, which regulate ribosomal gene transcription by modifying chromatin

structure to control accessibility to ribosomal DNA genes.

There are many open questions remaining in terms of the cellular response and adaptation

to 1CM perturbation, particularly in the context of cellular fitness. Through our studies, we


<!-- Page 159 -->


95

identified many potential connections for exploring the regulation of cellular fitness during folate

deprivation at the level of the ribosome and translation.

Intersections between folate metabolism and cellular stress responses

Our studies revealed many potential connections between the cellular response to folate

depletion and various stress responses. We can assess the role of the heat shock response (HSR),

integrated stress response (ISR), unfolded protein response (UPR), and the DNA damage response

(DDR). Folate is essential for the maintenance of healthy cells, and future work could reveal a

broad impact of folate scarcity on cellular stress. Importantly, our experiments were completed

primarily in erythroid cells (K562), and future studies could include expanding to other cell types

to further assess the impact of folate deprivation on overall human cellular biology.

The heat-shock response is induced by heat, but also by other environmental factors,

including nutrient depletion, as this stress response helps maintain proteostasis6. In the CRISPR

screen, HSF2 and HSF4 KO improves cell survival in low folate. HSF2 and HSF4 are essential

for development and differentiation processes. Moreover, KO of HSPA8 (Hsp70 isoform) resulted

in improved cell survival in low folate. This isoform is typically constitutively expressed. This is

an interesting connection because the encoded protein is crucial for maintaining proteostasis since

it is involved in protein folding, trafficking, and degradation. It is also a key component of

chaperone-mediated autophagy, where it binds to proteins and transports for lysosomal

degradation7. Additionally in the CRISPR screen, the KO of HSPA1A and HSPA1B (highly

inducible Hsp70 isoforms), resulted in decreased cell survival in low folate. Hsp70 is necessary

for the folding of new synthesized and misfolded proteins, and also facilitates the degradation of

damaged proteins by the ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal system8. Interestingly, it has also been


<!-- Page 160 -->


96

shown that Hsp70 phosphorylation exerts anti-apoptotic properties upon serum starvation in

hepatocellular carcinoma. This stress response is known to regulation stress tolerance, proteostasis,

and coordination of the cell between the HSR and autophagy9. These preliminary results may

indicate a broad coordination of the cell to ameliorate proteotoxicity induced by folate deprivation.

Nutrient deprivation, in particular amino acid deficiency, triggers the ISR. Therefore, we

could expect that folate deprivation may induce the ISR. From the CRISPR screen, we do not see

major changes in cell survival in low folate when the following ISR biomarkers are KO: GDF15,

PSME4, SQSTM1, ATF4. However, assessing these biomarkers via the screen does not give a

complete picture. Since the ISR works through the phosphorylation of EIF2a (resulting in a

decrease in global protein synthesis, to conserve energy and reduce further accumulation of

misfolded proteins), it would be best to investigate this pathway more directly through western

blotting. We could assess EIF2a phosphorylation, ATF4, CHOP, and PERK to give us a better

picture of ISR activation.

Nutrient deprivation (for example glutamine or glucose starvation) can induced the DDR,

sensing DNA damage and initiating repair mechanisms. However, our results in Chapter 2 show

that low folate depletion does not induce the DDR as shown through no significant increase in

phosphorylated CHK1 and no significant increase in γH2AX by Day 4 of folate depletion. KO

biomarkers of the DDR do not result in major increases or decreases in cell survival in our low

folate CRISPR screen.

Inhibiting 1CM by targeting SHMT1 or MTHFD2 is shown to induce cell stress by the

depletion of purines and glycine- which we show in chapter 2 also occurs through 1CM

perturbation by folate depletion. This was shown to induce the UPR in glioblastoma10 as well as

hepatocellular carcinoma cells11 through the upregulation of ATF4, but the direct link has not been


<!-- Page 161 -->


97

shown in K562. Our CRISPR results do not show a connection between the UPR and survival of

cells in low folate, however a better technique for assessing this connection would be qPCR or

western blotting to determine changes in mRNA and protein levels of UPR markers in cell

deprived of folate.

Cell-type dependence of stress responses to folate deprivation

We expect stress responses and genetic dependencies under low folate to be partly cell-type

specific and partly conserved. For example, we observe increased heme synthesis specifically in

erythroid cells (Chapter 2), which reflects their uniquely high demand for hemoglobin production

and coordinated erythroid differentiation programs. K562 cells are rapidly proliferating and retain

the capacity for erythroid differentiation, including inducible globin expression and active iron

metabolism, though these features are less pronounced than in primary erythroid cells. All of these

characteristics may shape how folate limitation is sensed and buffered.

At the same time, some responses to low folate are likely shared across cell types, particularly

those linked to core metabolic stress. For instance, our data show depletion of purine pools

(Chapter 2), which is expected to impact nucleotide balance, replication, and growth signaling.

Consistent with prior work by Hoxhaj et al., such metabolic stress may converge on nutrient-

sensing pathways like mTOR, which broadly regulate anabolic demand in response to metabolite

availability12.

Thus, while erythroid-specific features (like heme synthesis, extreme translational demand)

may drive unique dependencies, we expect key aspects of the response (such as nucleotide

depletion and nutrient sensing) to generalize across cell types.


<!-- Page 162 -->


98

Analysis of published UFMylation interaction datasets suggests a link between UFMylation and

cellular metabolic regulation

As an emerging PTM with diverse roles, recent high-throughput studies have mapped the

UFMylation interactome using IP-MS, identifying 337, 706, and 887 potential interactors13-15. A

previous lab member, Adam Maynard, compared these datasets to identify shared targets. ACLY,

ARL1, and NDUFA4 were the only three proteins in common across all three studies. None of

these have yet been confirmed as bona fide UFMylation substrates. Notably, ACLY and NDUFA4

are both linked to cellular metabolism. ATP citrate lyase (ACLY) is a cytosolic enzyme that

converts citrate and CoA into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. It acts as a crucial bridge between

carbohydrate metabolism and lipogenesis, providing acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis,

cholesterol biosynthesis, and histone acetylation. NDUFA4 is a subunit of complex IV of the

mammalian electron transport chain16. Although there are only 3 proteins shared across all three

published data sets, there are many more potential metabolic targets of UFMylation to explore.

Therapeutic opportunities at the intersection of UFMylation and folate metabolism

Our findings suggest a potential clinical implication for antifolate response and resistance.

Because inactivation of the UFMylation pathway confers a proliferative advantage under low-

folate conditions, tumors with reduced UFMylation activity may be relatively more tolerant of

folate stress and could therefore be less sensitive to antifolates such as methotrexate.

UFL1 promotes tumor growth in pancreatic cancer by enhancing the UFMylation of PARP1,

which stabilizes it and suppresses the DDR17. However, in prostate cancer18, liver cancer (HCC)

19, and CRC20, reduced UFMylation, particularly through the loss of the enzyme UFL1, promotes

cancer progression, metastasis, and immune evasion.


<!-- Page 163 -->


99

This raises the possibility that UFMylation status could serve as a biomarker for antifolate

response, although that remains to be tested directly. Methotrexate works by inhibiting DHFR and

blocking folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis. It is already used to treat several malignancies,

those of hematologic origin, like leukemias and lymphomas, as well as osteosarcoma, breast

cancer, head and neck cancer, and gestational trophoblastic diseases (such as choriocarcinoma).

Our data also raise the possibility that tumors with high anabolic demand, including some

mTOR-activated tumors, may be vulnerable to folate limitation, since purine depletion is expected

to constrain mTOR-linked growth programs. Some related work has shown that inhibition of

folate-mediated 1CM can suppress mTORC1 signaling and promote leukemic differentiation21.

The first questions to address about how inactivating UFMylation gives cells a growth

advantage under low folate are mechanistic: Does UFMylation loss alter methotrexate sensitivity,

and is this effect seen across multiple cell or cancer types or only in specific lineages? Therefore,

the most informative next studies would be cell-line panels and xenograft or genetically engineered

mouse models in which folate intake can be controlled. Those experiments will test whether

UFMylation-deficient tumors are resistant to antifolates, whether mTOR activation predicts

sensitivity, and whether dietary folate modifies treatment response. If those preclinical studies are

convincing, that would justify further planning towards a biomarker-driven clinical trial.

Next steps and caveats in clonal UFM1 knockout K562 cells

In the future, we plan to continue experiments using the clonal KOs of UFM1 in K562. First,

we would perform proliferation assays to measure cell doubling times under low folate conditions.

Based on the screen, we expect knockout cells to survive better than wild-type cells. However, the

screen was conducted in large volumes over ~14 doublings, whereas our standard experiments are


<!-- Page 164 -->


100

performed in smaller volumes (5-25 mL, most typically ~10 mL). Cell behavior can vary with

culture conditions as cells sense their environment and each other, so even at the same cell density,

differences in volume can influence growth and phenotype.

In addition, the response to low folate appears to be time-dependent. We observe distinct

changes at early versus later time points (Chapter 2), suggesting that cells adapt over time.

Furthermore, single-cell clones often adopt unexpected mutations. They are selected for being able

to grow from a single cell into a clonal population, an abnormal condition for cells. Often, these

cells will behave differently than a WT or KO population that is heterogenous.  Therefore, we

might expect that they may adapt differently in response to low folate than the cells used for the

screen.

A natural next step in clonal UFM1 knockout K562 cells would be to perform glycomics and

proteomics under low folate conditions. Glycomics is especially interesting because recent work

from a post-doc in the lab, Peng Wang, showed that folate depletion can alter glycan structures,

and also induces the UPR in T cells.  T cells require a surface glycocalyx for development,

activation, proliferation, and differentiation22. However, the glycocalyx covers all cells (the

glycans are attached to proteins and lipids) and acts as a critical molecular interface for cell

identification, signaling, adhesion, and protection. There is a known association between

glycosylation and the UPR23, but the connection with folate depletion is not yet published.

This is relevant because our RNAseq also suggested differential regulation of genes connected

to ER stress and protein homeostasis under low folate conditions. Testing whether UFM1 KO

changes glycosylation patterns or UPR activation could help connect the low-folate phenotype to

these specific stress-response pathways.


<!-- Page 165 -->


101

Lessons learned and considerations for future studies

Our approach to this project was to begin by investigating the major known substrate of

UFMylation based on the literature, RPL26. This was a limiting approach because we did not know

whether RPL26 was the main substrate of UFMylation in our system and did not know what else

might be UFMylated in K562 in low folate. Since we now have data showing that UFMylation of

RPL26 might not be a major target in our system, we can move on to find other potential targets.

A suggested approach moving forward could be to cross reference UFMylation proteomics data

and our CRISPR or RNASeq data sets to find new UFMylation candidates until we can perform

our own proteomics experiments.

This is an exciting new chapter for this project, as there are many potential connections to

investigate, and will lead to a better understanding of the link between UFMylation and folate

metabolism.

M. Haﬁz Rothi 1,2,6, Gautam Chandra Sarkar 3,4,6, Joseph Al Haddad 2,6, Wayne Mitchell5, Kejun Ying 1,2, Nancy Pohl 1,2, Roberto G. Sotomayor-Mena1,2, Julia Natale2, Scarlett Dellacona1,2, Vadim N. Gladyshev 5 & Eric Lieberman Greer 1,2,3,4

Specialized ribosomes help determine which proteins are synthesized, however, the inﬂuence of age on ribosome heterogeneity and whether dysregulation of this process drives organismal aging is unknown. Here we examined the role of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) methylation in maintaining appropriate translation as organisms age. In a directed RNAi screen, we identiﬁed 18S rRNA N6’-dimethyl adenosine (m6,2A) methyltransferase, dimt-1, as a regulator of C. elegans lifespan and stress resistance. We demonstrate that DIMT-1 functions in the germline after mid-life to regulate lifespan. Depletion of dimt-1 leads to selective translation of transcripts important for stress resistance and lifespan regulation in the C. elegans germline including the cytochrome P450 daf-9, which synthesizes a steroid that signals from the germline to the soma. dimt-1 induced lifespan extension is dependent on the daf-9 signaling pathway. Our ﬁndings highlight ribosome heterogeneity, and speciﬁc rRNA modiﬁcations, in maintaining appropriate translation later in life to promote healthy aging.

Disruption of the proteome is a hallmark of aging. Protein homeostasis or proteostasis is maintained by the processes of regulated protein degradation and production. There is increased dysregulation of protein homeostasis with age, and its misregulation can lead to protein aggregation diseases, including Alzheimer’s and Huntington’s diseases1,2. Depletion of the ribosome or attenuation of protein synthesis have been shown to increase lifespan in yeast, C. elegans, and Drosophila3–6. Research of the past two decades has focused on understanding how aggregation, degradation, shuttling, and translation have regulated proteostasis and how they go awry during aging or diseases7–11. Having the capacity to express the appropriate protein in response to environmental cues is an essential and evolutionarily conserved process. Therefore, preserving the proteome is critical for maintaining organismal health and healthy aging. However, how aging-responsive mRNAs are selectively translated is unknown.

More than 100 distinct post-transcriptional chemical modiﬁcations, termed the “epitranscriptome”, have been identiﬁed in cellular RNAs of all kingdoms of life12,13. The identiﬁcation of these residues, as well as the enzymes that add, remove, and recognize the modiﬁed bases, has revealed added complexity that controls virtually every aspect of RNA processing14–18. Ribosomal modiﬁcations help specify which transcripts are translated under different environmental conditions19–21, providing an additional layer of control to gene regulation. Ribosomal RNAs (rRNA; 28S, 18S, 5.8S, and 5S in eukaryotes) are encoded by many copies of ribosomal DNA throughout the genome, which display tissue-speciﬁc expression patterns22, raising the possibility that different combinations of rRNAs and ribosomal proteins could form ribosomes that are specialized for translation of subsets of mRNAs23. Some of these modiﬁcations (2’-O-methylation and pseudouridinylation) occur in substoichiometric frequency24,25, suggesting that specialized ribosomes might regulate differential

Historically, ribosomes were believed to translate whatever transcript they were presented with, but recent studies suggest that ribosome composition varies and plays a signiﬁcant role in the regulation of translation. Whether rRNA methylation becomes dysregulated during aging and could play a role in preserving proteome integrity as organisms age is still unclear. We have recently demonstrated that the N6-dimethyladenosine (m6,2A) methyltransferase, DIMT-1, which methylates adenosines 1735 and 1736 on 18S rRNA, regulates selective ribosomal binding and translation of speciﬁc mRNAs to regulate intergenerational transmission of the response to ancestral starvation26. However, whether rRNA methylation more broadly can regulate age and stress-responsive translation and how this dysregulation drives the aging process is still unknown. Here, we performed a directed RNAi screen of all putative rRNA methyltransferases to identify whether rRNA methyltransferases could regulate lifespan and stress resistance in the nematode C. elegans. We also examined how rRNA methylation changes with age. We found that the 18S rRNA m6,2A methyltransferase, dimt-1, regulates C. elegans lifespan and stress resistance. Lifespan extension induced by dimt-1 deﬁciency required the known regulator of mRNA translation, the Rag GTPase, raga-1. Using an auxin-inducible degron-tagged version of dimt-1, we demonstrate that DIMT-1 functions in the germline after mid-life to regulate lifespan. We further found that knockdown of dimt- 1 leads to selective translation of transcripts important for stress resistance and lifespan regulation in the C. elegans germline in mid-life, including the cytochrome P450 daf-9, which synthesizes a steroid that signals from the germline to the soma to regulate lifespan. We found that dimt-1-induced lifespan extension was dependent on the daf-9 signaling pathway. This ﬁnding reveals an additional layer of proteome dysfunction, beyond protein synthesis and degradation, as an important regulator of aging. Our ﬁndings highlight ribosome heterogeneity, and speciﬁc rRNA modiﬁcations, in maintaining appropriate translation later in life to promote healthy aging.

Results dimt-1 rRNA methyltransferase knockdown extends lifespan and increases resistance to stress Previous genome-wide RNAi screens for genes that regulate lifespan in C. elegans have been performed in worms where progeny production was inhibited27–29, which has been shown to mask the effect of some genes on lifespan30,31. An understudied aspect of proteostasis during aging is ribosome heterogeneity, and one of the key factors for heterogeneity are rRNA modiﬁcations such as methylation, which are catalyzed by rRNA methyltransferases. Hence, we performed a targeted RNAi screen for putative rRNA methyltransferases present in fertile C. elegans to test whether manipulation of rRNA methylation could regulate lifespan or stress resistance. We knocked down 26 putative rRNA methyltransferases and discovered that knockdown of several rRNA methyltransferases could signiﬁcantly shorten or extend C. elegans lifespan (Fig. 1a). As previously reported32, knockdown of T01C3.7/ﬁb-1 extended C. elegans lifespan (~9% p < 0.0005, Fig. 1a). FIB- 1 is a homolog of the 2’-O-methyltransferase ﬁbrillarin, which is conserved in animals and plants. We also found that knockdown of E02H1.1/dimt-1 caused the most signiﬁcant extension of lifespan (22–33% p < 0.0001) (Fig. 1a). We had previously reported that DIMT-1 is the 18S rRNA N6-dimethyladenosine (m6,2A) methyltransferase for adenosines 1735 and 1736 in C. elegans26. DIMT-1 is a conserved methyltransferase that methylates conserved adjacent adenosines on the 18S rRNA in yeast and humans33–35. Although lifespan extension can be beneﬁcial, it may also come with detrimental effects to the organism. To determine if the effects on longevity by rRNA methyltransferase knockdown were associated with improved health, we performed UV stress and heat stress survival

rRNA modiﬁcations are dynamically regulated throughout the lifespan Although we found that rRNA methyltransferases regulate lifespan and stress resistance, it was still unclear whether rRNA modiﬁcations themselves change during the life of the organism. Changes in speciﬁc modiﬁcations with age may indicate a regulatory role for rRNA methylation events. We ﬁrst wanted to see if the rRNA methyltransferase genes are dynamically expressed during the life of C. elegans. Examination of previously published transcriptional proﬁles of C. elegans during aging43, revealed that a number of putative rRNA methyltransferases are dynamically expressed with age (Supplementary Fig. 2a). There were genes which are strongly expressed in early life and declined towards the end, such as ZK1128.2/mett-10, W01B11.3/nol-58, and W07E6.1/nsun-1. Alternatively, genes such as E02H1.1/dimt-1 and C18A3.1/damt-1 showed the opposite trend, peaking near the end of the lifespan (Supplementary Fig. 2a). We independently conﬁrmed that E02H1.1/dimt-1 expression increases as C. elegans age (Supplementary Fig. 2b), suggesting that knockdown of dimt-1 is reverting the worm to a more youthful state. To test if the rRNA modiﬁcations themselves showed similar patterns during aging, we performed ultra-high performance liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS) with wild-type (WT) N2 worms harvested in an age gradient at days 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, and 19. We measured rRNA modiﬁcation levels in the 26S and 18S rRNA subunits in four biological replicates. We observed a similarly dynamic pattern of change in rRNA modiﬁcations across lifespan

(Fig. 2a). 2’-O-ribose methylation increased on all four nucleosides (Am, Cm, Gm, Um) as the worm gets older in both the 26S and 18S rRNAs (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2c). Other 18S rRNA modiﬁcations such as m6A and surprisingly, m6,2A, showed the inverse trend with a higher level in early life which declines as the worm ages (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2c). Since knockdown of the 18S rRNA m6,2A methyltransferase, dimt-1, increased C. elegans lifespan, we had hypothesized that m6,2A would have increased as C. elegans age. This ﬁnding could suggest a dynamic and either a tissue or cell-speciﬁc change in 18S rRNA m6,2A, which might be masked by examination of changes in rRNA methylation across all tissues. It could also reﬂect that the age gradient was generated under conditions using the drug 5-ﬂuorodeoxyuridine (FUdR), which inhibits proliferation of germline stem cells, the production of intact eggs in adults, and extends longevity30,44 which could affect the m6,2A levels. These results suggest that both rRNA methyltransferases and modiﬁcations are dynamically regulated throughout the lifespan of C. elegans. We had found that the lifespan extension phenotypes observed from the RNAi screen is sometimes associated with increased stress resistance in survival assays (Fig. 1). We wanted to determine if there were associated changes in rRNA methyltransferases and modiﬁcations when C. elegans are exposed to stress. When we examined a previously published transcriptomic dataset21, we found that most rRNA methyltransferases decreased expression in response to 37 °C heat stress (Supplementary Fig. 2d). We found that rRNA modiﬁcations in wild-type N2 worms were less consistently dynamic in response to 37 °C heat shock or UV stress exposure (Fig. 2b, c). Some rRNA modiﬁcations did change in response to the stresses, for example, 2’-Oribose adenosine methylation (Am) in 26S rRNA was signiﬁcantly increased and 2’-O-ribose cytosine methylation (Cm) in 18S rRNA subunit was signiﬁcantly decreased in response to heat stress (Supplementary Fig. 2e). We also observed a signiﬁcant increase in 2’-Oribose guanosine methylation (Gm) and Am in 26S rRNA in response to UV exposure (Supplementary Fig. 2f). As with the changes in rRNA methylation during aging (Fig. 2a), lack of changes in speciﬁc rRNA methylation in response to stress could reﬂect tissue-speciﬁc changes, which change in opposite directions in different tissues or an inability to capture the correct window to observe changes due to dynamic

We generated a catalytically inactive DIMT-1 by mutating the conserved glutamic acid E79 to alanine, that we had previously

demonstrated was necessary for DIMT-1’s catalytic activity in vitro26. Therefore, DIMT-1 methyltransferase activity is required for lifespan and stress resistance regulation.

We found that dimt- 1 knockdown increased lifespan to a similar extent in mutants of the acetylcholine receptor, eat-2, which has reduced pharyngeal pumping and therefore decreased food intake, and has been proposed as a genetic mimic of dietary restriction47,48 (23.65% in WT, 30.55% in eat-2; p = 0.7021 by two-way ANOVA, Fig. 3c). Next, we tested if daf-16, which is a FOXO transcription factor that mediates longevity regulation downstream of several signaling pathways8,51–56, has an effect on dimt-1 knockdown-induced lifespan extension. We found that dimt-1 knockdown extended wild-type worm lifespan but failed to increase the lifespan of daf-16 mutant C. elegans (p = 0.0907), indicating that daf-16 is functioning in the same genetic signaling pathway as dimt-1 (23.65% in WT, 5.13% in daf-16; p < 0.0001 by two-way ANOVA, Fig. 3f). We also tested raga-1, which is a Rag GTPase that links amino acid sensing to mechanistic target of rapamycin complex (mTORC)1, where raga-1 mutation causes an increase in lifespan57. Again, dimt-1 knockdown increased WT worm lifespan but failed to increase the long lifespan of raga-1 mutant worms (22.67% in WT, 0.53% in raga-1, p = 0.0327 by two-way ANOVA, Fig. 3g), suggesting that DIMT-1 functions in the same signaling pathway as RAGA-1 and TOR. To determine if an intact germline is necessary for dimt-1 induced lifespan extension, we performed dimt-1 knockdown in glp-1(e2141ts) mutant worms, which develop 5–15 meiotic germ cells instead of ~1500 when shifted to the restrictive temperature58 and pgl-1(bn101ts) mutant worms, which have defective germ granules and are sterile59. Knockdown of dimt-1 extended the lifespan of WT worms but failed to increase the lifespan of either glp-1(e2141ts) or pgl-1(bn101ts) mutant worms (28.32 or 40.16% in WT, −5.23% in glp-1, 3.34% in pgl-1; p < 0.0001 by two-way ANOVA, Fig. 3h, i), suggesting that a functional germline is required for the dimt-1 knockdown induced lifespan extension. Taken together, these results show that dimt-1 is likely affecting or regulating lifespan through the DAF-16 and TOR pathways and either functions in or requires the germline for longevity regulation.

DIMT-1 functions in the germline to regulate lifespan To resolve the paradox of depletion of dimt-1 extending lifespan while 18S rRNA m6,2A decreases in whole worms with age (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2c), we next wished to determine whether DIMT-1, which is a ubiquitously expressed protein, was functioning in speciﬁc tissues to regulate lifespan. To examine DIMT-1’s tissue-speciﬁc function, we created an auxin-inducible degron (AID) tagged DIMT-1 worm strain and crossed it with strains that express TIR1 in a tissue-speciﬁc manner to allow for tissue-speciﬁc auxin-dependent depletion of DIMT-160,61. We found that DIMT-1 depletion ubiquitously led to a signiﬁcant decrease in 18S rRNA m6,2A relative to control strains as assessed by UHPLC-MS/MS, suggesting that our AID-tagged DIMT-1 strains were effective (Fig. 4a). We found that when DIMT-1 was depleted using two independent ubiquitous eft-3 promoters or the germline-speciﬁc mex-5 promoter to drive TIR1 expression we observed a signiﬁcant lifespan extension relative to control AID-tagged DIMT-1 strains that did not express TIR1 (29.71% p < 0.0001 and 47.97% p < 0.0001 respectively, Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 3b). In contrast, we observed no lifespan extension when DIMT-1 was depleted in muscle, intestine, or neurons (Fig. 4b). This ﬁnding suggests that DIMT-1 not only requires the presence of a functional germline to regulate lifespan (Fig. 3h, i), but indeed functions in the germline to regulate lifespan.

To validate our ﬁndings from the AID/TIR1 experiments, we performed an orthogonal approach by using tissue-speciﬁc RNAi strains to knock down dimt-1 and measure its effect on lifespan. When we speciﬁcally knocked down dimt-1 in muscle, intestine, or neurons, we failed to observe a signiﬁcant increase in lifespan; however, germline-speciﬁc knockdown of dimt-1 caused a signiﬁcant increase in lifespan that was comparable to knockdown of dimt-1 in WT worms (16.93% in WT, 15.93% in germline-speciﬁc; p = 0.8536 by two-way ANOVA, Fig. 4c, d). Further bolstering the importance of the germline for the longevity effects of dimt-1, we found that treating worms with 5-ﬂuorodeoxyuridine (FUdR), which inhibits proliferation of germline stem cells, the production of intact eggs in adults, and extends longevity30,44, abolished the effect of dimt-1 knockdown on lifespan (Fig. 4e). This ﬁnding could also explain why, in our aging gradient, which out of technical necessity was generated using FUdR, we observed a decrease in 18S rRNA m6,2A levels (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2c).

DIMT-1 affects ribosome binding to speciﬁc mRNA transcripts in the germline We had previously found that knockdown of dimt-1 in the parental generation caused a signiﬁcant misregulation of both transcription and ribosome binding to transcripts involved in the determination of adult lifespan in the eggs of progeny26. Presumably, all effects on transcription come as a secondary consequence of alterations in translation. To speciﬁcally examine which transcripts displayed altered binding by ribosomes after a decrease in DIMT-1 at later stages of life in the germline, we performed germline-speciﬁc Translating Ribosome Afﬁnity Puriﬁcation (TRAP)62,63 in four independent biological replicates from worms that were grown on empty vector (EV) control or dimt-1 RNAi. We used a ﬂag-tagged RPL-4 driven by the germlinespeciﬁc promoter mex-5, which has previously been shown not to have a negative effect on ribosome function63. We ﬁrst validated that dimt-1 knockdown extended longevity in this strain (Supplementary Fig. 3c). We next analyzed the transcription changes in response to dimt-1 knockdown in post reproduction worms. Transcriptional changes would not be predicted to be direct consequences of manipulating the rRNA methylation; however, a natural consequence of changes in translation will lead to changes in transcription64,65. We found that 5765 genes were differentially expressed, with 3700 genes that were signiﬁcantly upregulated and 2065 genes that were signiﬁcantly downregulated upon dimt-1 depletion compared to the empty vector control (Supplementary Fig. 4a and Supplementary Data 1). Pathway analysis revealed increased expression of genes involved in longevity regulation, xenobiotic detoxiﬁcation, TGF-β, WNT, and MAPK signaling pathways, as well as degradation pathways including proteasome, peroxisome, and autophagy genes (Supplementary Fig. 4b, c and Supplementary Data 1). Downregulated genes were enriched for protein processing, mTOR and FOXO/DAF-16 signaling pathway, and ribosome biogenesis genes (Supplementary Fig. 4d, e and Supplementary Data 1). These altered transcriptional pathways could help to explain the extended longevity in response to dimt-1 depletion, and the decreased expression of FOXO/DAF-16 and mTOR signaling pathways expression could help explain the daf-16 and raga-1 dependency of the lifespan extension (Fig. 3f, g). As RAGA-1 is a RAG GTPase that links amino acid sensing to the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex mTORC1, these ﬁndings suggest that raga-1 dependency is mediated by both transcriptional and translational changes induced by dimt-1 depletion. To determine if dimt-1 depletion also altered the ribosome binding levels of speciﬁc transcripts, we sequenced ribosome-bound RNAs from the same four biological replicates isolated from the germline by TRAP and normalized them to the levels of the transcripts to measure translation efﬁciency. Discussion Here, we show that DIMT-1, an evolutionarily conserved 18S rRNA m6,2A methyltransferase26,34,35,72, regulates lifespan in C. elegans. Reduction of DIMT-1 causes a lifespan extension that requires the DAF-16/FOXO transcription factor and TOR signaling. We found that DIMT-1 functions in the germline to regulate C. elegans lifespan and also causes differential binding of the ribosome to speciﬁc subsets of mRNA transcripts. One of the altered transcripts we identiﬁed was daf-9, and we found that reduction of DIMT-1 caused a lifespan extension that required both the cytochrome P450 enzyme DAF-9 and its

downstream nuclear hormone receptor transcription factor DAF-12. These results suggest an overall model whereby DIMT-1 regulates organismal lifespan by selective translation in the germline of speciﬁc mRNA transcripts, which subsequently leads to altered germline-tosoma signaling and lifespan. Furthermore, while most longevity regulators identiﬁed to date function early in life to “lock-in” aging rates, we found that DIMT-1 can regulate lifespan after middle age. Together, this study provides evidence of selective translation, via ribosome heterogeneity, playing a signiﬁcant role in the regulation of aging. A major feature of aging is the loss of proteostasis, where maintenance of the appropriate amounts of proteins in the cell, is signiﬁcantly disrupted later in life73,74. Previous studies have examined the levels of misfolded proteins, which become increasingly prevalent in older organisms, causing breakdown of normal cellular function75,76. However, little is known about how transcripts are selected for translation during the aging process. Ribosomes were initially believed to be non-discriminatory, translating any mRNA transcripts they were presented with77, but recent work has suggested that specialized ribosomes can translate unique sets of transcripts under speciﬁc stress conditions21,23,78–80. We found that perturbations in many of the enzymes that regulate rRNA modiﬁcations have substantial effects on overall health and duration of lifespan in C. elegans (Fig. 1). We26, and others81, have recently shown that DIMT-1’s function to N6-dimethylate two adjacent adenines on the 18S rRNA can direct the ribosome to speciﬁc subsets of transcripts for translation. Our previous work suggests that while DIMT-1 binding to rRNAs during rRNA processing is important for the appropriate processing of rRNAs, the decreased expression of dimt-1 that we see in response to dimt-1 knockdown is not sufﬁcient to signiﬁcantly alter rRNA processing26.
